2027-04-04.title: New Sunday · The Lord Appears to Thomas
readings: Peace be with you; receive the Holy Spirit
Elijah taken up; Elisha receives his spirit
The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God
Here is your God; he will feed his flock
A living hope through the resurrection
Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead
2027-04-04.alt: New Sunday, the first Sunday after Qyomtho.
2027-04-04.verse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
theo: On the evening of Easter the disciples are behind locked doors, afraid. Jesus comes and stands among them: “Peace be with you.” He shows them his hands and side, and they rejoice. Then he sends them: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you,” breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them.” From the first Easter evening the risen Lord gives his Church peace, mission, the Spirit and the power to forgive sins.

Thomas was not there. When the others say, “We have seen the Lord,” he answers: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.” A week later Jesus comes again and says: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.” And Thomas makes the greatest confession of faith in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!”

For us in India this Gospel is our own story. Thomas, who doubted and then believed, brought that faith to our land. The Church of Malankara, like all the St Thomas Christians, received from him the confession “My Lord and my God.” His doubt became our certainty; his wounded hand-touch became our faith.

Jesus adds a word for all later generations: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” That is us. St Peter says: “Although you have not seen him, you love him… and rejoice with an indescribable and glorious joy.” New Sunday asks: do we live with the joy of believers, or with the fear of locked doors?
conn: The breath of life.
As God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the risen Christ breathes the Spirit into his disciples: a new creation.
Elijah and Elisha.
Elisha asks for a double share of Elijah's spirit (2 Kings 2:9); the apostles receive the Spirit of the risen Lord.
Joseph raised up.
Joseph, rejected by his brothers, is raised over Egypt to save them (Genesis 41): a figure of the risen Christ.
The wounds remain.
The risen body keeps its wounds: signs of love that last for ever (Revelation 5:6).
altar: Thomas touched the wounds; we receive the wounded and risen Body at the Holy Qurbono. Many in our tradition whisper Thomas' words at the elevation: “My Lord and my God.”
outline: Opening
Locked doors and fearful hearts.
Point 1 · Peace, mission, Spirit, forgiveness
The risen Lord's first gifts to his Church.
Point 2 · Thomas' doubt
Honest questions brought to Jesus become faith.
Point 3 · Our Apostle
St Thomas and the faith of India: “My Lord and my God.”
Point 4 · Blessed are those who have not seen
Living faith and joy today.
Take-home line
“My Lord and my God!”
live: Pray Thomas' prayer
At the elevation in Holy Qurbono, and each morning, say: “My Lord and my God.”
Receive his peace (John 20:19)
Bring a fear or a locked door of your heart to Jesus in Confession.
Share your faith
Tell one person how you came to believe.
fathers: St Gregory the Great
The disbelief of Thomas was of more benefit to our faith than the faith of the believing disciples; when he touched and believed, every doubt was removed from our minds (Homilies on the Gospels 26).
St Augustine
He saw and touched the man, and confessed the God whom he did not see and touch (Tractates on John 121).
magis: Catechism 644–645
The apostles' faith was born of the encounter with the risen Lord; Jesus invited them to touch his body, which kept the marks of the Passion.
Catechism 1441–1442
The risen Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive sins in his name.
Catechism 448
The title “Lord” confesses the divinity of Jesus; Thomas' confession is its high point.
saints: Hevoro week ends. 11 April: the Second Sunday after Qyomtho.
2027-04-04.prayer: Lord Jesus, risen and wounded, you came through locked doors and gave your disciples peace. Breathe your Spirit on us, heal our doubts, and make us confess with St Thomas, our father in faith: My Lord and my God! Amen.

2027-04-11.title: Second Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: Do you love me? Feed my sheep
The song of Moses at the sea
God raised him from the dead
Pray in the Spirit at all times
The risen Lord by the Sea of Tiberias
2027-04-11.verse: Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.”
theo: After the Resurrection Peter says, “I am going fishing,” and the others go with him. They fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a stranger on the shore says: “Cast the net to the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” The net fills so full they cannot haul it in. The beloved disciple says: “It is the Lord!” Peter jumps into the sea to reach him.

On the shore Jesus has already made a charcoal fire, with fish and bread. “Come and have breakfast.” The risen Lord of glory cooks for his tired friends. He meets them in their ordinary work, in their failure, and feeds them. Every Holy Qurbono is this breakfast on the shore: the risen Lord takes bread and gives it to us.

Then, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus heals Peter's wound. Three times Peter had denied him by a fire in the high priest's courtyard; three times Jesus asks: “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Three times Peter answers: “Lord, you know that I love you.” And three times Jesus entrusts him: “Feed my lambs… tend my sheep… feed my sheep.” Failure is not the end; love restores and sends.

Moses sang at the sea: “The LORD is my strength and my might, and he has become my salvation.” Wisdom says: “God did not make death.” Paul preaches in Antioch: “God raised him from the dead.” The risen Christ turns empty nights into full nets, and denials into love.
conn: The full net.
153 large fish (John 21:11): the Fathers saw in the unbroken net the Church gathering all nations without being torn.
Two charcoal fires.
Peter denied Jesus by a charcoal fire (John 18:18) and is restored by another (John 21:9).
The song of the sea.
Exodus 15: the first Easter song, sung after passing through the waters, as we pass through Baptism.
God did not make death.
Wisdom 1:13; God created for life, and in Christ restores it.
altar: “Come and have breakfast.” Jesus “took the bread and gave it to them” (John 21:13): the same gestures as at the Last Supper and Emmaus. At every Qurbono the risen Lord invites us to his table on the shore.
outline: Opening
Empty nets: nights of failure.
Point 1 · “It is the Lord!”
Recognising Jesus in ordinary life.
Point 2 · Breakfast on the shore
The risen Lord serves and feeds: the Eucharist.
Point 3 · “Do you love me?”
Peter restored; our failures healed by love.
Point 4 · Feed my sheep
Love becomes service: pray for our pastors.
Take-home line
“Lord, you know that I love you.”
live: Answer the question
Each night this week answer Jesus: “Lord, you know that I love you.”
Begin again
Return to a good practice you abandoned after a failure.
Pray for the Pope and bishops
Pray for Peter's successor and our Catholicos, shepherds of the flock.
fathers: St Augustine
The threefold confession of love answers the threefold denial, so that his tongue might serve love no less than fear (Tractates on John 123).
St Gregory the Great
The disciples returned to fishing, which was not sin; but the Lord met them at their work, to show that he calls us in the midst of our daily labour (Homilies on the Gospels 24).
magis: Catechism 553, 881
Jesus entrusted to Peter a specific authority: to feed his sheep; the Pope is Peter's successor.
Catechism 1429
Peter's conversion after his triple denial bears witness to Jesus' infinite mercy.
Catechism 1347
The Eucharistic meals with the risen Lord (Emmaus, the shore) are signs of his presence.
saints: Weekdays of the season of Qyomtho. 18 April: III Sunday after Qyomtho.
2027-04-11.prayer: Risen Lord, you met your disciples after a night of failure, filled their nets and fed them on the shore. Feed us at your table, heal our denials with your love, and send us to care for your flock. Lord, you know that we love you. Amen.

2027-04-18.title: Third Sunday after Qyomtho · The Road to Emmaus
readings: He appeared in another form to two of them
Yet you did not return to me
I was ready to be found
By grace you have been saved
2027-04-18.verse: Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road, while he was opening the scriptures to us?
theo: On Easter afternoon two disciples walk away from Jerusalem towards Emmaus, sad and confused. “We had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel.” Jesus himself comes near and walks with them, but their eyes are kept from recognising him. He listens to their sorrow, then opens the Scriptures: “beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the things about himself in all the scriptures.”

As evening falls they beg him: “Stay with us, because it is almost evening.” At table “he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him.” They had heard him in the Word; they recognise him in the breaking of the bread. Emmaus is the shape of every Holy Qurbono: first the Word that sets hearts burning, then the Bread in which we know him.

The two disciples do not wait until morning. That same hour they return to Jerusalem to tell the others: “The Lord has risen indeed.” A heart that has met the risen Lord cannot stay silent. Peter and John say the same before the council in Acts: “we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

St Paul reminds us that this is all grace: “by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” Jesus walks with us on our roads of disappointment, even when we do not recognise him. He waits to be invited: “Stay with us.”
conn: Moses and the prophets.
Jesus reads the whole Old Testament as pointing to him (Luke 24:27): the reason our lectionary reads Law and Prophets every Sunday.
The breaking of the bread.
Took, blessed, broke, gave: the words of the Last Supper (Luke 22:19) and of every Qurbono.
Another form.
Mark 16:12: the risen Lord appears “in another form”; we must learn to recognise him.
I was ready to be found.
Isaiah 65:1: God seeks those who were not seeking him.
altar: The Liturgy of the Word and the Holy Qurbono are Emmaus repeated every Sunday: our hearts burn as the Scriptures are opened, and our eyes are opened at the breaking of the bread.
outline: Opening
Walking away from Jerusalem: our disappointments.
Point 1 · He walks with us
Even unrecognised, the Lord is near.
Point 2 · Hearts burning
The Word opened: read Scripture with Christ as its key.
Point 3 · Known in the breaking of the bread
The Qurbono: Word and Bread.
Point 4 · Return and tell
“We cannot keep from speaking.”
Take-home line
“Stay with us, Lord.”
live: Read the Gospel daily
Read the Sunday Gospel each day this week and ask Jesus to open it to you.
Invite him
Pray each evening: “Stay with us, Lord, for it is evening.”
Tell someone
Share with one person a time when you felt the Lord walking with you.
fathers: St Augustine

They did not recognise him while he explained the Scriptures; they recognised him in the breaking of the bread. So we too, who do not see him in the flesh, recognise him in the breaking of the bread (Sermon 235).
St Gregory the Great
They invited the stranger to share their home, and found God; by hospitality they came to know the One they had not known in the explanation of the Scriptures (Homilies on the Gospels 23).
magis: Catechism 1346–1347
The Eucharistic liturgy unfolds like the Emmaus meal: the Word, then the breaking of bread.
Dei Verbum 21
The Church has always venerated the Scriptures as she venerates the Body of the Lord, offering the bread of life from the table of the Word and of the Body.
Verbum Domini 54
The Emmaus story shows the unity of Word and Eucharist.
saints: 23 Apr: St George, Martyr. 25 Apr: St Mark, Evangelist (falls on Sunday in 2027).
2027-04-18.prayer: Lord Jesus, you walked with the disciples of Emmaus and made their hearts burn as you opened the Scriptures. Walk with us on our roads, open the Word to us, make yourself known in the breaking of the bread, and stay with us, for it is evening. Amen.

2027-04-25.title: Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: Go and make disciples of all nations
In a time of favour I have answered you
A new creation; ambassadors for Christ
You are witnesses of these things
2027-04-25.alt: Season of Qyomtho. In the 2025–26 lectionary this Sunday was Syro-Malankara Catholic Laity Day. Today is also the feast of St Mark the Evangelist.
2027-04-25.verse: And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
theo: The risen Lord stands among his frightened disciples: “Peace be with you… Why are you frightened, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself.” He eats before them. Then “he opened their minds to understand the scriptures”: the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and “repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations… You are witnesses of these things.”

In the evening Gospel the risen Christ gives the great commission on a mountain in Galilee: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything that I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” The Church exists to evangelise.

Peter discovers in the house of Cornelius that “God shows no partiality”: the Gospel is for every nation. St Paul calls every Christian an ambassador: “if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation… So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us.” This is why the Church honours the laity today: the mission is not only for priests and religious, but for every baptised person in family, work and society.

Job's fortunes were restored when he prayed for his friends; Solomon received wisdom when he asked for it. Let us ask the risen Lord for the wisdom and courage to be his witnesses, knowing that he is with us always.
conn: To all nations.
Isaiah 49:6, “a light to the nations”, is fulfilled when the risen Christ sends his disciples to all peoples (Luke 24:47; Matthew 28:19).
Touch and see.
The risen body is real: hands, feet, eating fish (Luke 24:39–43). The Resurrection is not a vision.
A new creation.
2 Corinthians 5:17: in Christ the new creation begun on Easter morning reaches every believer.
Prayer for friends.
Job 42:10: Job is restored when he prays for the friends who had wronged him.
altar: At the end of every Holy Qurbono the priest blesses and sends us out. That dismissal is the great commission: we leave the altar as witnesses, with the promise “I am with you always.”
outline: Opening
Peace to frightened hearts.
Point 1 · Real resurrection
Touch and see; he eats with them.
Point 2 · Minds opened
Christ is the key to the Scriptures.
Point 3 · Go, make disciples
The great commission belongs to all the baptised: Laity Day.
Point 4 · I am with you always
Courage for witness.
Take-home line
“You are witnesses of these things.”
live: Be an ambassador (2 Corinthians 5:20)
Speak one word of faith or hope to a colleague or neighbour this week.
Serve in the parish
Offer your time to one parish ministry or lay association.
Pray for missionaries
Pray for priests, sisters and lay missionaries from Kerala working in North India and abroad.
fathers: St Leo the Great
Christ showed them his wounds so that the marks of the nails and the spear might heal the wounds of unbelieving hearts (Sermon 73 on the Ascension, 2).
St John Chrysostom
He did not say “I will be with you only”, but “with all who believe after you”; he spoke to all the faithful as to one body (Homilies on Matthew 90).
magis: Apostolicam Actuositatem 2–3
The Christian vocation is by its nature a vocation to the apostolate; the laity share in the priestly, prophetic and kingly office of Christ.
Christifideles Laici 15
The lay faithful are called to sanctify the world from within, in family, work and society.
Catechism 849–856
The missionary mandate: the Church is sent to all nations.
saints: 25 Apr: St Mark the Evangelist. 29 Apr: St Catherine of Siena. 1 May: St Joseph the Worker. 2 May: St Athanasius of Alexandria.
2027-04-25.prayer: Risen Lord Jesus, you opened the minds of your disciples and sent them to all nations. Open our minds to the Scriptures, make us your ambassadors in our families and work, and keep us faithful to your promise: I am with you always. Amen.

2027-04-01.title: Thursday of Hevoro week · Easter Thursday
readings: We do see Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death
He is God not of the dead, but of the living
2027-04-01.alt: Hevoro week, the first week of the season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection). Hevoro means white: the week is kept as one great day of Easter joy, and it closes with New Sunday. Today the Church hears the Lord's own answer to those who denied the resurrection.
2027-04-01.verse: He is God not of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong.
theo: Christ is risen! In the white week of Easter the Church sets before us a question that was once meant as a trap. “Some Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to him.” They tell of a woman married in turn to seven brothers, each of whom died, and ask: “In the resurrection whose wife will she be?” The story is built to make the hope of rising look foolish. Jesus does not mock them; he shows them where they went astray: “Is not this the reason you are wrong, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?” Many of the Jewish people of his day, with the Pharisees, already believed that God would raise the dead, as the prophets and the Maccabean martyrs had hoped (Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7:9). Jesus stands with that faith of Israel and deepens it. The risen life is not this life repeated; “when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.” This does not make marriage small. Marriage belongs to this age as a sacrament of Christ's love for his Church, and it points beyond itself to the wedding feast of the Lamb, where every love that was faithful is fulfilled, not cancelled (Catechism 1619–1620).

Then the Lord goes to the book of Moses itself, to the burning bush. God said, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” He did not say “I was.” Long after the patriarchs had been buried, God still named himself by them, because they were alive to him. “He is God not of the dead, but of the living.” The Letter to the Hebrews shows how this hope reaches us. It quotes Psalm 8: God made human beings “for a little while lower than the angels” and crowned them “with glory and honor.” Then it admits honestly: “As it is, we do not yet see everything in subjection to them, but we do see Jesus, who for a little while was made lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.” What Psalm 8 promised to humanity is already true in one Man, the risen Jesus. St Irenaeus wrote that the glory of God is a human being fully alive, and that true life is to see God (in substance). On Easter morning that glory shone first in the body of Christ, and in him it is promised to us.

How do we live this Thursday of Hevoro week? First, speak of our departed with Easter words. When we remember parents, grandparents and friends who have died, let us say what Jesus says: God is their God still, and they are alive to him. Pray for them at the Holy Qurbono, and light the lamp at home for them this evening with an Easter hymn. Second, honor marriage as a road to heaven. Husbands and wives can pray together tonight for the grace to love each other in a way that will not be ashamed on the last day. Third, when someone laughs at the faith with a clever question, answer as the Lord did: patiently, from the Scriptures, and with trust in the power of God. Hevoro week continues until New Sunday, when the Church will hear how the risen Lord showed his wounds to Thomas.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I think of those I love who have died, do I think of them as dead or as living to God?
Point 1 · The question built as a trap
Seven brothers, one wife, and a mistake about God.
Point 2 · The God of the living
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are alive to him.
Point 3 · We do see Jesus
Psalm 8 fulfilled in the risen Lord.
Take-home line
“He is God not of the dead, but of the living.”
live: Pray for the departed with Easter hope (Mark 12:27)
This evening light the lamp, name your departed one by one, and say: “They are alive to you, Lord.”
Look to Jesus crowned (Hebrews 2:9)
When something in life is not yet as it should be, say quietly: “We do not yet see everything, but we do see Jesus.”
2027-04-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you are the God not of the dead but of the living. For a little while you were made lower than the angels, and you tasted death for everyone; now you are crowned with glory and honor. Keep us faithful to the Scriptures and confident in the power of God. Give rest and light to our departed, who are alive to you. Bless husbands and wives, and lead every family to the wedding feast of your kingdom. To you be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The One who tasted death for everyone and is now crowned with glory gives himself to us in the Holy Qurbono: his risen Body and Blood, the pledge that we too shall live.

2027-04-02.title: Friday of All the Confessors (Sakala Mawdyanmar) · Friday of Hevoro week
readings: Of whom the world was not worthy
Everyone who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge
2027-04-02.alt: Hevoro week, the first week of the season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection). Hevoro means white: the week is kept as one great day of Easter joy, and it closes with New Sunday. The Panchangam names this Friday after the Resurrection the day of All the Confessors (സകല മൗദ്യാനന്മാർ).
2027-04-02.verse: Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.
theo: Christ is risen! On the first Friday after Qyomtho the Church does not return to the Friday of the Cross alone; she keeps the memory of all the confessors. In the Syriac tradition a mawdyono, a confessor, is one who confessed Christ openly before others and bore the cost: prison, exile, torture, and for many, death. The Panchangam calls this day the Friday of All the Confessors (Sakala Mawdyanmar). It is fitting that they are remembered in the white week. On Good Friday the Lord went down into death; on this Friday we honor those who followed him there and now share his victory. The Book of Revelation sees them “robed in white” before the throne, having “washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” Hevoro, the white week of the newly baptized, is also the week of the white robes of the witnesses. The Letter to the Hebrews names some of the heroes of faith of the old covenant and then lists those whose names it does not give: “Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned to death, they were sawn in two, they were killed by the sword.” Then comes a sentence that every age of persecution has repeated with gratitude: they were people “of whom the world was not worthy.”

Why did they not deny Christ? Today's Gospel gives the Lord's own reasons. First, nothing stays hidden: “What I say to you in the dark, tell in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim from the housetops.” Second, the worst that persecutors can do has a limit: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” Third, we are known and loved in every detail: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. And even the hairs of your head are all counted. So do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.” And finally, a promise: “Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.” Tertullian told the rulers of his time that the blood of Christians is seed: the more they were mown down, the more they grew (in substance). Hebrews ends with a mystery: those heroes “did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better so that they would not, apart from us, be made perfect.” The confessors of every age wait to be made perfect together with us, in the one Body of the risen Christ.

How do we keep the Friday of All the Confessors? Remember the confessors of our own land: St Thomas the Apostle, who according to the tradition of our Churches gave his life for Christ in India; and the Christians of our own time in India and elsewhere who have lost homes, health or life rather than deny the Lord. Pray today for all who suffer for the faith, and if you can, give to a fund that helps persecuted Christians. Ask the Virgin Mary, whom the Church invokes as Queen of Confessors, for courage. Then look at your own day: where am I silent about Christ out of fear of laughter or of losing favor? A word at the office, a sign of the cross before a meal in a restaurant, a Sunday kept holy against pressure: these are small confessions, and the Lord who counts the hairs of our head does not forget them. Come to the Holy Qurbono, where the risen Lord whom the confessors acknowledged gives himself to us.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did I last speak of Christ when it would have been easier to stay silent?
Point 1 · Of whom the world was not worthy
The heroes of Hebrews 11 and the confessors of every age.
Point 2 · Do not be afraid
The sparrows and the hairs of our head.
Point 3 · Acknowledge me before others
Small confessions and a great promise.
Take-home line
“Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven.”
live: Pray for the persecuted (Hebrews 11:36–38)
Pray today by name for a country or a community where Christians suffer for their faith; give something, if you can, to help them.
Make one small confession (Matthew 10:32)
Today, in a place where it costs you a little, make the sign of the cross or say a word about Christ without shame.
2027-04-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen and glorious, you promised to acknowledge before your Father everyone who acknowledges you before others. We thank you for all the confessors who held fast to you in chains, in exile and in death, of whom the world was not worthy. Through their prayers strengthen the Christians who suffer for your name today. Deliver us from the fear that keeps us silent, and teach us that we are of more value than many sparrows. With the Virgin Mary, Queen of Confessors, and all your witnesses, we praise you with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The confessors drew their strength from the Body and Blood of the Lord; in the Holy Qurbono the same risen Christ strengthens us to confess him before others.

2027-04-03.title: Saturday of Hevoro week · Easter Saturday
readings: Christ was faithful over God's house as a son, and we are his house
Do not stop him; whoever is not against you is for you
2027-04-03.alt: Hevoro week, the first week of the season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection). Hevoro means white: the week is kept as one great day of Easter joy, and it closes with New Sunday. This is the last day of the white week; tomorrow is New Sunday.
2027-04-03.verse: Christ, however, was faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house if we hold firm the confidence and the pride that belong to hope.
theo: Christ is risen! On the last day of Hevoro week the Letter to the Hebrews invites us to look steadily at Jesus: “Therefore, brothers and sisters, holy partners in a heavenly calling, consider that Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, was faithful to the one who appointed him.” Two titles are joined here. Jesus is the apostle, the one sent from the Father to us; and he is the high priest, the one who goes from us to the Father, carrying our humanity into the sanctuary of heaven. In his Death and Resurrection both movements are complete. The letter then compares him with Moses, whom God himself had praised: “Not so with my servant Moses; he is entrusted with all my house” (Numbers 12:7). Hebrews honors Moses fully; he “was faithful in all God’s house as a servant.” But Jesus “is worthy of more glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.” Moses served inside the house; Christ is the Son over the house, and with the Father he is its builder. The comparison is not a contest between two faiths. It is the joy of the Church that the faithfulness of Moses finds its fulfillment in the faithfulness of the Son.

And what is this house? “We are his house if we hold firm the confidence and the pride that belong to hope.” The house of God is not first of all a building of stone, but the people whom the risen Lord gathers. St Augustine told his people at the dedication of a church that the building is the house of our prayers, but we ourselves are the house of God, being built in this life and dedicated at the end of time (in substance). The Gospel shows how easily we forget this. John, the beloved disciple, reports with some pride: “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” Jesus answers: “Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you.” The house of God is larger than our little circle. Moses had once answered Joshua in the same spirit when two men prophesied outside the camp: “Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!” (Numbers 11:29). The Second Vatican Council teaches that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the visible structure of the Catholic Church, and that they belong by right to the one Church of Christ (Unitatis Redintegratio 3; Lumen Gentium 8). We hold the fullness of the faith with gratitude, and we rejoice in every good done in the name of Jesus.

How do we close Hevoro week? Thank God today for the house he is building: your parish, your family, your prayer group, and the whole Church. Hold firm the confidence of hope. If the joy of Easter has already faded in you after a few days, ask the Lord to renew it before New Sunday. Look around for good that others are doing in Jesus' name, perhaps a neighboring parish of another Church, a youth group, a charity, and instead of competing, thank God and help them. Prepare for tomorrow's Holy Qurbono on New Sunday, when the risen Lord will say again to his disciples, “Peace be with you,” and Thomas will confess, “My Lord and my God!” If you can, go to confession today, so that you enter New Sunday with a clean heart.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I think of the Church as a building I visit, or as a house I am part of?
Point 1 · Consider Jesus
Apostle and high priest of our confession.
Point 2 · We are his house
Moses the faithful servant and Christ the Son.
Point 3 · Do not stop him
The house of God is larger than our circle.
Take-home line
“We are his house if we hold firm the confidence and the pride that belong to hope.”
live: Hold firm the hope (Hebrews 3:6)
Before New Sunday, ask the Lord in a short prayer to renew the joy of Easter in you.
Rejoice in good done in Jesus' name (Luke 9:50)
Thank God aloud for one good work done by people outside your own group, and help it if you can.
2027-04-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, apostle and high priest of our confession, you were faithful to the Father who appointed you, and you are the Son over God's house. Make us your house: living stones, built together in faith, firm in the confidence and pride of hope. Deliver us from jealousy when others do good in your name, and enlarge our hearts to rejoice in every work of your Spirit. Prepare us for New Sunday, that with Thomas we may confess you, our Lord and our God. To you be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Our High Priest, faithful over God's house, gathers his household at the altar; in the Holy Qurbono he builds us into one house by giving us his own Body and Blood.

2027-04-05.title: Monday after New Sunday · Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead
readings: Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead; the word of God is not chained
The parable of the vineyard: the stone that the builders rejected
2027-04-05.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after New Sunday.
2027-04-05.verse: Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, a descendant of David
theo: Christ is risen! The day after New Sunday, St Paul speaks to us from a prison cell. He writes to Timothy: “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, a descendant of David.” This is the shortest summary of the Gospel in the New Testament, and it is written by a man in chains. He suffers hardship, “even to the point of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God is not chained.” Paul knows that he may soon die; the letter is his farewell. Yet he does not ask Timothy to remember Paul. He asks him to remember Jesus, alive. To remember, in the Bible, is not only to think of something past; it is to let the living God act now. That is why the Lord said at the Supper, “Do this in remembrance of me.” Each Holy Qurbono is this living memory: the risen Christ, of David's line, truly present with his Body and Blood. Then Paul quotes what may be an early Christian hymn: “The saying is sure: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he will also deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.” Even our unfaithfulness cannot undo his faithfulness. St Ignatius of Antioch, led in chains to Rome to die, wrote seven letters on the way that are still read today; his body was bound, but the word he preached could not be bound.

The Gospel tells the parable of the vineyard. A man plants a vineyard with care, fences it, digs a wine press, builds a tower, and leases it to tenants. When he sends servants for his share, they beat and kill them. Last of all he sends “a beloved son,” thinking, “They will respect my son.” But the tenants say, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” They kill him and throw him out of the vineyard. The vineyard is a picture of God's people from Isaiah 5; the servants are the prophets; the beloved son is Jesus himself, telling his own Passion before it happens. Mark notes that those who heard it “realized that he had told this parable against them,” that is, against the leaders who were already planning his death, while the crowd listened to him gladly. The Church teaches that the guilt for the Lord's death cannot be laid on all the Jews of that time or on the Jewish people of any later time (Catechism 597; Nostra Aetate 4). The parable is a warning to every steward of God's vineyard in every age, including those who lead the Church today: the vineyard is the Lord's, not ours. And it ends with Easter: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is amazing in our eyes.” The Son who was thrown out has been raised up as the foundation of the new temple.

How do we live this Monday of Qyomtho? Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, at the start and end of the day: say those words slowly when you wake and before you sleep. Think of the vineyard entrusted to you: your family, your work, your gifts, your share in the parish. Ask: am I giving the Lord his share, or treating it as mine? If you have been rejected or pushed aside, take heart from the stone that the builders rejected; the Lord can build on what others throw away. Pray for prisoners, especially those in prison for their faith, and for prison chaplains. And if you feel that you have been faithless since Easter, hear Paul's word: he remains faithful. Come back to him in confession and at the Holy Qurbono.
outline: Opening
Ask: what do I remember first each morning?
Point 1 · The word of God is not chained
Paul in prison, remembering the risen Christ.
Point 2 · He remains faithful
The early hymn of dying and living with him.
Point 3 · The stone that the builders rejected
The vineyard, the beloved son, and Easter.
Take-home line
“Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead.”
live: Remember the risen Christ (2 Timothy 2:8)
Say slowly, on waking and before sleep, “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead.”
Give the Lord his share (Mark 12:2)
Choose one part of your time, money or gifts this week and give it consciously to God.
2027-04-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, you are the beloved Son sent to the vineyard, rejected and killed, and raised up as the cornerstone. Teach us to remember you each day as the living Lord. Make us faithful tenants of all you have entrusted to us, and give you the fruit that is yours. When we are faithless, you remain faithful: draw us back to you. Strengthen all who are in chains for your name, for your word is not chained. To you be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: “Do this in remembrance of me”: in the Holy Qurbono the Church remembers Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, and he is truly present, the cornerstone on which we are built.

2027-04-06.title: Tuesday after New Sunday · Made alive together with Christ
readings: By grace you have been saved; created in Christ Jesus for good works
He rebuked the fever; immediately she got up and began to serve them
2027-04-06.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after New Sunday.
2027-04-06.verse: But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ
theo: Christ is risen! In the Easter season the Church reads St Paul's letter to the Ephesians, which speaks of Easter as something that has already happened to us. “You were dead through the trespasses and sins in which you once lived.” Paul does not soften the picture: without Christ, we were following “the course of this world,” ruled by our passions, and “by nature children of wrath, like everyone else.” Then come two words that change everything: “But God.” “But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ… and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.” What God did for Jesus on Easter morning, he has begun in us through Baptism. We were buried with him, we were raised with him, and in hope we are already seated with him. “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not the result of works, so that no one may boast.” Salvation is pure gift; no one earns the first grace (Catechism 1996–1998, 2010).

Yet Paul at once adds: “For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.” The Catholic faith holds both together: we are saved by grace, not by our own works; and grace is not idle, it makes us capable of works of love that God himself has prepared for us. The Gospel shows this in a small household scene. Jesus enters Simon's house after the synagogue. Simon's mother-in-law has a high fever. “Then he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. Immediately she got up and began to serve them.” The Greek word for “got up” is the same family of words used for the Resurrection; healed by the Lord, she rises and serves. St Jerome, preaching on this scene in Mark's Gospel, prayed that the Lord would come into our house too, and with a word heal the fever of our sins, so that we might rise at once and serve him (in substance). Then, at sunset, the whole town brings its sick, and “he laid his hands on each of them and cured them.” Not the crowd in general, but each one. He silences the demons who shout his name, because he will not be proclaimed by them; he will be known through the Cross and the empty tomb.

How do we live this Tuesday of Qyomtho? First, thank God for the grace of Baptism: you were dead, but God made you alive with Christ. If you know the date of your Baptism, mark it in your calendar this year. Second, ask the Lord to rebuke whatever fever burns in you: anger, envy, anxiety, an addiction. Name it before him and, if it is sin, bring it to confession. Third, rise and serve. Simon's mother-in-law did not wait to feel stronger; she began at once. Do one good work today that God has prepared for you: help at home without being asked, visit someone sick, take food to a family in need. Bring a sick person you know to the Lord in prayer at the Holy Qurbono, as the people of Capernaum did at sunset.
outline: Opening
Ask: what would my life be without the words “But God”?
Point 1 · But God, rich in mercy
Dead through trespasses, made alive with Christ.
Point 2 · She got up and served
The Lord rebukes the fever and raises up for service.
Point 3 · Created for good works
Saved by grace for a life of love.
Take-home line
“But God, who is rich in mercy… made us alive together with Christ.”
live: Thank God for your Baptism (Ephesians 2:5)
Find out the date of your Baptism, and this evening thank God that he made you alive together with Christ.
Rise and serve (Luke 4:39)
Do one service today at once, without waiting to be asked or to feel like it.
2027-04-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, when we were dead through our trespasses the Father, rich in mercy, made us alive together with you. Come into our house as you came into Simon's house. Stand over us and rebuke every fever of sin and fear, and raise us up to serve you at once. Lay your hands on each of the sick we bring to you, and heal them. Make us live the good works you have prepared for us, so that no one may boast except in your grace. To you be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the risen Lord enters our house as he entered Simon's; receiving his Body and Blood, we are raised up to serve.

2027-04-07.title: Wednesday after New Sunday · He is our peace
readings: He is our peace; he has broken down the dividing wall
The lamp on the lampstand; pay attention to how you listen
2027-04-07.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after New Sunday.
2027-04-07.verse: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
theo: Christ is risen! On Easter evening the risen Lord stood among his frightened disciples and said, “Peace be with you.” Today St Paul explains how deep that peace goes. He writes to Christians who were not born Jews: “Remember that you were at that time without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.” Notice what Paul honors here: the commonwealth of Israel and the covenants of promise are a treasure. Gentile believers, which is to say almost all of us, have been brought near to Israel's hope, grafted, as Paul says elsewhere, onto the olive tree whose root supports us (Romans 11:17–18). The Church remembers with gratitude her spiritual bond with the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4). Then the great sentence: “For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.” When Paul says that Christ “abolished the law with its commandments and ordinances,” he is speaking of the rules that kept Jew and Gentile apart as a wall; he does not mean that God's commandments no longer matter. Christ fulfills the Law, and in him both have “access in one Spirit to the Father.” Here is the whole Trinity in a single line, and the Cross is the place where hostility was put to death.

What walls still stand among us? Families divided over property, neighbors who have not spoken for years, the old wounds of caste that still mark some Christian communities in Kerala, suspicion between Churches that share one Baptism. Christ has already broken the wall in his flesh; our part is to stop rebuilding it. Our own Church knows something of this grace: in 1930 Mar Ivanios and his companions entered full communion with the Bishop of Rome, and the Syro-Malankara Church still prays daily for the unity of all Christ's disciples. The Gospel adds a word about how this peace spreads. “No one after lighting a lamp hides it under a jar, or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.” The light of Easter is not for hiding. Then Jesus says something sharp: “Then pay attention to how you listen; for to those who have, more will be given; and from those who do not have, even what they seem to have will be taken away.” The one who listens with faith receives more; the one who hears without receiving loses even the little he thought he had. St Augustine told his hearers that the sound of the preacher's words strikes the ear, but the true Teacher is within, and only he makes the word take root (in substance).

How do we live this Wednesday of Qyomtho? Look honestly for one wall in your life: a relative, a neighbor, a colleague, a Christian of another Church you have kept at a distance. Take one step toward them this week: a greeting, a phone call, a visit, a prayer said for them by name. Pray for the unity of Christians, especially among the Churches of the St Thomas tradition in Kerala. And watch how you listen: at the Holy Qurbono, try to hear the readings as if for the first time; at home, switch off the screen for ten minutes and let the Gospel speak; with others, listen to understand rather than to answer. The lamp is lit; let it stand on the lampstand of a peaceful life.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there a wall in my life that Christ has broken but I keep rebuilding?
Point 1 · Brought near by the blood of Christ
Far and near, Gentile and Jew, in the commonwealth of promise.
Point 2 · He is our peace
The dividing wall broken down in his flesh.
Point 3 · Pay attention to how you listen
The lamp on the lampstand and the listening heart.
Take-home line
“For he is our peace.”
live: Take one step across a wall (Ephesians 2:14)
Choose one person you have kept at a distance and greet, call, visit, or pray for them by name this week.
Listen to receive (Luke 8:18)
Before the readings at the Holy Qurbono, pray: “Lord, let me hear this as if for the first time.”
2027-04-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you are our peace. In your flesh you made both groups into one and broke down the dividing wall of hostility; through you we all have access in one Spirit to the Father. Bring near all who are far off, heal the divisions in our families, our parishes and our Churches, and keep us from rebuilding the walls you have broken. Set the lamp of your Easter light on the lampstand of our lives, and teach us to listen to your word with faith, so that more may be given us. To you be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the risen Lord, who is our peace, gathers those who were far and those who were near into one Body, and in the Holy Qurbono he gives us the peace that no wall can keep out.

2027-04-08.title: Thursday after New Sunday · Memory of Most Rev. Lawrence Mar Ephrem
readings: Remember your leaders; Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever
The faithful and wise servant whom the master finds at work
2027-04-08.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after New Sunday. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Most Rev. Lawrence Mar Ephrem (died 1997), a bishop of our Church, and gives John 10:11–18 as an alternative Gospel (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 49).
2027-04-08.verse: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
theo: Christ is risen! Eleven days after Qyomtho the Church opens the last chapter of the Letter to the Hebrews and hears a command that fits a memorial day: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.” Today the Panchangam remembers Most Rev. Lawrence Mar Ephrem, a bishop of our Church who died in 1997. To remember a bishop is not to keep a photograph on the wall. The letter asks for three things: remember those who spoke God's word to you, look at how their lives ended, and copy their faith. Then it gives the reason that makes such remembering possible: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The shepherds pass; the Chief Shepherd does not. The bishop who laid his hands on a priest, the priest who baptized a child, the catechist who taught her the Creed: all of them handed on one Lord, risen and alive, who is today what he was on the morning of the Resurrection. This is why the Church prays for her departed bishops and gives thanks for them in the Holy Qurbono: their work was his work, and he has not changed.

The Gospel puts a question to every leader and to every disciple: “Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?” A steward does not own the house. He is given charge of it, and his task is to feed the household on time. “Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.” The wicked servant says to himself, “My master is delayed,” and turns the trust into a chance to beat others and to feast. St Gregory the Great, writing on the shepherd's care, said that the one placed over others is first a servant of their needs (in substance). The alternative Gospel shows the same thing from the shepherd's side: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” The food the household needs most is the word of God and the Bread of life. A bishop, a priest, a parent and a teacher are all stewards in their measure, and the master who will come is the risen Lord himself.

Hebrews then speaks of the altar: “We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.” Jesus “suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood,” and from that sacrifice comes the food of the Church. The Fathers read this altar as the table of the Lord's Body and Blood, where the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present and we truly receive him (Catechism 1362–1367). From the altar the letter sends us out: “Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.” Here is how to keep this Easter week: come to the Holy Qurbono, praise God with your lips, and share what you have. Say a prayer today for the bishops who have served our Church and gone to their rest, and for the bishops who serve us now. Ask the risen Lord to make you a faithful steward of whatever he has placed in your hands.
outline: Opening
Ask: who first spoke the word of God to me, and have I thanked God for that person?
Point 1 · Remember your leaders
Remember, consider, imitate.
Point 2 · The faithful steward
Food for the household at the proper time.
Point 3 · The altar and the sacrifice of praise
We eat at his altar and go out to share.
Take-home line
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
live: Remember your leaders (Hebrews 13:7)
Pray today by name for a bishop, priest or teacher who brought you the faith, living or departed.
Do good and share (Hebrews 13:16)
Share one thing you have this week with someone who needs it, quietly, as a sacrifice pleasing to God.
2027-04-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the same yesterday and today and forever, the Good Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep and took it up again. We thank you for the shepherds who spoke your word to us, and we remember today your servant Lawrence Mar Ephrem; grant him rest in the light of your face. Make our bishops and priests faithful and wise stewards, who feed your household at the proper time. Feed us at your altar, and teach us to offer you a sacrifice of praise and to share what we have. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar of the Holy Qurbono we eat from the sacrifice of Christ who suffered outside the gate; from there we go out to offer God the sacrifice of praise and of sharing.

2027-04-09.title: Friday after New Sunday
readings: God was pleased to reveal his Son to me; the persecutor now proclaims the faith
The least among you is the greatest
2027-04-09.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after New Sunday.
2027-04-09.verse: But when God, who had set me apart before I was born and called me through his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles, I did not confer with any human being.
theo: Christ is risen! The Resurrection did not stop with the Eleven in the upper room. Some years later the risen Lord met a man who was hunting his disciples, and today St Paul tells the Galatians what happened to him. He hides nothing: “You have heard, no doubt, of my earlier life in Judaism. I was violently persecuting the church of God and was trying to destroy it.” He was zealous, gifted, ahead of his companions. Then everything turned, and not by his own effort: “But when God, who had set me apart before I was born and called me through his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles...” Notice the words. God set him apart, God called him, God was pleased to reveal his Son. Paul saw the risen Christ on the road to Damascus (Acts 9; 1 Corinthians 15:8), and he counts himself among the witnesses of the Resurrection. Paul does not reject his people or their faith; he speaks with respect of “the traditions of my ancestors” and later says that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). His zeal was turned, not destroyed: the same fire that once persecuted would now carry the Gospel to the ends of the earth.

What did the newly called Paul do? Not what we might expect. “I did not confer with any human being, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were already apostles before me, but I went away at once into Arabia, and afterwards I returned to Damascus.” Only “after three years” did he go up “to visit Cephas and stayed with him fifteen days.” A conversion needs hidden years. The Lord himself spent thirty years in Nazareth before three years of preaching. St John Chrysostom remarks that Paul went to Peter not to be taught as a beginner but to honour him as the first of the apostles (in substance). And the end of the passage is beautiful: the churches of Judea “only heard it said, ‘The one who formerly was persecuting us is now proclaiming the faith he once tried to destroy.’ And they glorified God because of me.” The best proof of the Resurrection is a changed life. When people who knew what we once were see what we have become, they do not praise us; they glorify God.

The Gospel brings us down from the great apostle to a small child. “An argument arose among them as to which one of them was the greatest.” Jesus does not argue back. He takes “a little child” and puts it by his side, and says, “Whoever welcomes this child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me; for the least among all of you is the greatest.” Paul learned this. The man who had been ahead of everyone called himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15:9). On this Friday of the Easter season, look honestly at your own past, as Paul did, without hiding it and without despair: the grace that turned Paul can turn anyone. Pray for someone you have given up on. Welcome a child, a newcomer or a person who seems unimportant as you would welcome Christ. And if an argument starts about who is greatest, at home, at work or in the parish committee, be the one who steps back.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there anyone I have decided can never change?
Point 1 · Called through grace
God set Paul apart and revealed his Son.
Point 2 · The hidden years
Arabia, Damascus, and fifteen days with Cephas.
Point 3 · The least is the greatest
A child placed at the Lord's side.
Take-home line
“And they glorified God because of me.”
live: Pray for one you have given up on (Galatians 1:23)
Name someone you think will never change, and pray for him or her every day this week.
Welcome the least (Luke 9:48)
Give your full attention today to a child or to someone others overlook.
2027-04-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you met Saul on the road and turned the persecutor into your apostle. You know our past, and your grace is stronger than all of it. Reveal yourself to us more deeply, and to all who are far from you. Give us the humility to welcome the least in your name, and let our changed lives lead others to glorify the Father. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The same risen Lord who appeared to Paul comes to us in the Holy Qurbono, to set us apart for himself and to send us out.

2027-04-10.title: Saturday after New Sunday
readings: Paul lays his gospel before the leaders in Jerusalem, so that the truth of the gospel might remain
Woe to Chorazin; whoever listens to you listens to me
2027-04-10.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after New Sunday. Tomorrow is the Second Sunday after Qyomtho.
2027-04-10.verse: Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me, and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.
theo: Christ is risen! Yesterday Paul told how the risen Lord called him; today he tells how he kept communion with the Church. “Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up in response to a revelation.” Fourteen years of preaching lay behind him, and still he laid his message before the leaders of the Church: “Then I laid before them (though only in a private meeting with the acknowledged leaders) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure that I was not running, or had not run, in vain.” Here is a great lesson for every gifted Christian. Paul had seen the risen Lord himself, yet he did not run alone. He submitted his preaching to the apostles, so that his work would be one with theirs. The Gospel is not a private discovery; it is received, guarded and handed on in the communion of the Church. St Irenaeus, writing a century later, pointed to this unbroken handing on through the bishops in the apostolic Churches as the sign of the true faith (in substance).

The question that troubled the young Church was whether Gentile believers like Titus had to be circumcised and keep the whole Law of Moses to belong to Christ. Paul's answer was clear, and the leaders in Jerusalem agreed with him: “But even Titus, who was with me, was not compelled to be circumcised, though he was a Greek.” Against “false believers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus,” Paul stood firm, “so that the truth of the gospel might always remain with you.” This freedom is not a freedom to do as we like. It is the freedom of children who are saved by the grace of the risen Christ, not by their own achievements, and who now live by his Spirit. Paul speaks here about what was required of Gentile converts, not against the Jewish people, whose covenant with God the Church honours (Catechism 839). And he adds a word every parish can use: “God shows no partiality.” In Christ there are no first-class and second-class members.

The Gospel is sober. Jesus grieves over the towns where he did his mighty works: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” Those towns had seen everything and changed nothing. The danger is not far from us. We have heard the Easter proclamation, received the Holy Qurbono, seen the light of the Resurrection. Then Jesus gives his messengers an astonishing dignity: “Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me, and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.” When the Church preaches the Gospel faithfully, it is Christ who speaks (Catechism 87). On Saturdays many of our families turn in prayer to the holy Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, who heard the word of God and kept it in her heart. Ask her today for a listening heart. Tomorrow, the Second Sunday after Qyomtho, come to the Holy Qurbono ready to listen, and ask the risen Lord to let his word change something in you this week.
outline: Opening
Ask: have I heard much and changed little?
Point 1 · Not running in vain
Paul lays his gospel before the apostles.
Point 2 · The freedom we have in Christ
Titus, the truth of the gospel, and a God who shows no partiality.
Point 3 · Whoever listens to you listens to me
Woe to the towns that saw and did not change.
Take-home line
“Whoever listens to you listens to me.”
live: Listen and change (Luke 10:13)
Choose one word from tomorrow's Holy Qurbono and put it into practice before next Saturday.
No partiality (Galatians 2:6)
Greet and speak with someone in your parish whom you usually ignore.
2027-04-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen and alive, you speak to us through your Church and send messengers in your name. Do not let us be like the towns that saw your mighty works and did not repent. Keep us in the communion of your apostles, guard in us the truth of the Gospel and the freedom you have won for us, and deliver us from all partiality. By the prayers of your holy Mother, give us hearts that listen and are changed. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The Lord who says “Whoever listens to you listens to me” speaks in the word proclaimed at the Holy Qurbono and gives himself in the Mysteries; let us hear him and receive him with changed hearts.

2027-04-12.title: Monday after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho · St Julius, Pope
readings: Peace with God; suffering produces endurance, character and hope
Whoever welcomes you welcomes me; a cup of cold water
2027-04-12.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho. Commemoration of St Julius, Pope (Julius I, Bishop of Rome 337–352).
2027-04-12.verse: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
theo: Christ is risen! The first gift of the risen Lord to his frightened disciples was peace: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). Today St Paul explains what that peace is. “Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand; and we boast in our hope of sharing the glory of God.” Peace with God is not first a calm feeling. It is a new relationship: the enmity of sin is ended, the door is open, and we stand in grace. Christ “was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification,” Paul has just written (Romans 4:25). Easter is the reason we can stand before God unafraid. Then Paul says something surprising: “And not only that, but we also boast in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint us, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.” Suffering does not cancel the peace of Easter; in Christ it becomes a road to hope.

Today the Panchangam commemorates St Julius, Bishop of Rome from 337 to 352. His years fell in the storm that followed the Council of Nicaea, when many powerful men sought to soften the faith that the Son is truly God, of one being with the Father. St Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria who defended that faith, was driven from his see, and he came to Rome. Julius received him, examined his case with a synod in Rome, declared him innocent, and wrote a firm letter to the Eastern bishops who had condemned him, asking why the matter had not been referred to Rome as custom required. Julius did not fear the anger of emperors or bishops; he welcomed the persecuted shepherd. The Gospel of the day reads like a portrait of him: “Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.” In welcoming Athanasius, Julius welcomed Christ, and helped to keep the faith of Nicaea, which we still confess in the Creed at every Holy Qurbono.

Jesus ends with the smallest gift: “and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, none of these will lose their reward.” The Fathers loved this verse. St John Chrysostom pointed out that the Lord said “cold” water, so that no one could say he was too poor even to light a fire (in substance). Welcome is within everyone's reach. It may be a refugee family in the next street, a migrant worker from the north at your bus stop, a priest newly transferred to your parish, a student far from home. To welcome them in Christ's name is to welcome Christ, and the Father who sent him. Pray today for the Pope and for all who suffer for the true faith. Then give one cup of cold water: a meal, a phone call, a seat, a word of welcome to someone who needs it. That is the peace of Easter going out from your heart.
outline: Opening
Ask: whom have I welcomed this Easter, and whom have I kept outside?
Point 1 · Peace with God
Justified by faith, we stand in grace.
Point 2 · Suffering that produces hope
Endurance, character, and a hope that does not disappoint.
Point 3 · Whoever welcomes you welcomes me
St Julius welcomed Athanasius; a cup of cold water.
Take-home line
“Whoever welcomes you welcomes me.”
live: Welcome in his name (Matthew 10:40)
Make one stranger or newcomer feel at home this week: a visit, a meal or a phone call.
Hope in suffering (Romans 5:3–5)
Offer one difficulty of this week to God, asking for endurance and hope.
2027-04-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you have given us peace with the Father and poured God's love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. By the prayers of St Julius, who welcomed your persecuted servant Athanasius and guarded the faith of Nicaea, keep our Pope and our bishops firm in the truth. Turn our sufferings into endurance and hope, and make us quick to welcome the least of your brothers and sisters, even with a cup of cold water. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: Through Christ we have access to the grace in which we stand; at the Holy Qurbono he welcomes us to his table, and sends us to welcome others in his name.

2027-04-13.title: Tuesday after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho · Mar Seraphion
readings: Christ, a priest forever, offered prayers with loud cries and tears and was heard
2027-04-13.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam commemorates Mar Seraphion today; it does not say which saint of that name is meant, so parishes keep the memory as their own calendar gives it.
2027-04-13.verse: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.
theo: Christ is risen! The Letter to the Hebrews today takes us back to the night before the Passion, and then forward to the Resurrection. “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.” We think of Gethsemane, where the Lord prayed, “Abba, Father, for you all things are possible; remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want” (Mark 14:36). And Hebrews says: he was heard. Not by being spared the Cross, but by being brought through death into the glory of the Resurrection. The Father's answer to the tears of Gethsemane was the empty tomb. This is a deep comfort for everyone who prays and seems not to be answered. The Son himself prayed with tears; he knows what it is. And the Father hears, often in a way we cannot see until later.

“Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered; and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been designated by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.” Christ did not make himself a priest: “Christ did not glorify himself in becoming a high priest, but was appointed by the one who said to him, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’” His priesthood is not like the old priesthood that passed from father to son and ended in death. Like Melchizedek, who brought out bread and wine (Genesis 14:18), Christ is “a priest forever.” Risen and ascended, he stands before the Father for us now. Every time the priest stands at the altar in the Holy Qurbono, he acts in the person of this one eternal High Priest, who offers himself and makes intercession for us (Catechism 1544–1548). Our Church has always loved this mystery: the Lord who is both the priest and the offering. Today the Panchangam also remembers Mar Seraphion, whose memory our calendar keeps among the saints; with all the saints he now shares in the prayer of the great High Priest.

The Gospel shows how the Son's prayer became ours. “He was praying in a certain place, and after he had finished, one of his disciples said to him, ‘Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.’” The disciples watched Jesus pray and wanted what he had. He gave them the words we still say: “Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us. And do not bring us to the time of trial.” To call God “Father” is possible only because the Son shares his own relationship with us; Tertullian called this prayer a summary of the whole Gospel (in substance). In our Church we say the Lord's Prayer at every hour of prayer and before Holy Communion in the Holy Qurbono. Pray it slowly today, at least once, thinking about each line. Ask yourself whom you need to forgive, and what “daily bread” you are anxious about. Then trust the Father, who heard the cries of his Son.
outline: Opening
Ask: have I ever prayed with tears, and how did God answer?
Point 1 · Loud cries and tears
Gethsemane, and the Father's answer in the Resurrection.
Point 2 · A priest forever
Appointed by the Father, after the order of Melchizedek.
Point 3 · Lord, teach us to pray
The Our Father, the prayer of sons and daughters.
Take-home line
“He was heard because of his reverent submission.”
live: Pray the Our Father slowly (Luke 11:2–4)
Once today, pray the Lord's Prayer as slowly as you can, stopping after each line.
Forgive (Luke 11:4)
Name one person you need to forgive, and pray for them by name.
2027-04-13.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, in the days of your flesh you prayed with loud cries and tears, and the Father heard you and raised you from the dead. You are our High Priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek, living always to make intercession for us. Teach us to pray as you prayed: to call God our Father, to seek his kingdom, to forgive as we are forgiven, and to trust him in every trial. By the prayers of Mar Seraphion and all the saints, keep us faithful. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: Christ, the High Priest forever, stands at the altar in the Holy Qurbono and offers himself to the Father for us; before Communion we pray with his own words, “Our Father.”

2027-04-14.title: Wednesday after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho · Mar Shemun Bar Sabbae
readings: Let us go on toward perfection; the ground that drinks the rain
The friend at midnight; ask, search, knock; the Father gives the Holy Spirit
2027-04-14.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho. Commemoration of Mar Shemun Bar Sabbae (Simeon bar Sabbae), bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon and martyr in Persia (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 50).
2027-04-14.verse: So I say to you, Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you.
theo: Christ is risen! In these weeks after Qyomtho, the newly baptized and all of us are tempted to settle down: the feast is over, Lent is behind us, life goes on as before. Hebrews refuses to let us stop. “Therefore let us go on toward perfection, leaving behind the basic teaching about Christ, and not laying again the foundation: repentance from dead works and faith toward God, instruction about baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.” The foundation is precious: repentance, faith, Baptism, the laying on of hands, the hope of the resurrection. But a foundation is laid in order to build. The Christian who received the risen Lord at Easter is called to grow, not merely to stay where he was. Then comes a hard warning about those who “have once been enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit,” and then fall away. The Church has never read this as if there were no forgiveness for sins after Baptism; she has always held that there is no sin so grave that the Church cannot forgive it, for those who repent (Catechism 982). The warning is against a deliberate turning away that refuses to come back: that heart, “holding him up to contempt,” closes the door on itself. The remedy is in the image that follows: “Ground that drinks up the rain falling on it repeatedly, and that produces a crop useful to those for whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God.” Easter is rain. Let it bear fruit.

Today the Panchangam commemorates Mar Shemun Bar Sabbae, known in the West as St Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, the twin royal city of the Persian Empire on the Tigris. In the fourth century, under King Shapur II, the Christians of Persia were suspected of siding with Rome. According to the ancient accounts, Shemun was ordered to collect a heavy double tax from his people and to bring them to worship the sun. He refused: he would not burden his poor flock, and he would worship only the God who made the sun. He was put to death with many bishops, priests and faithful, on a Good Friday, around 341 to 344, at the start of a long persecution. The historian Sozomen tells that an old court official named Usthazanes, who had once been a Christian and had given way under pressure, was moved by the bishop's courage, confessed Christ again, and died a martyr before him. There is Hebrews 6 in a single life: a man who had fallen away, given grace to return, and ground that at last bore fruit. The Syriac Churches have kept the memory of the Persian martyrs with love, and our own liturgy belongs to the same Syriac tradition in which their story was first told.

The Gospel gives the secret of such strength: persistent prayer. Jesus tells of a man who goes to a friend at midnight and says, “Friend, lend me three loaves of bread; for a friend of mine has arrived, and I have nothing to set before him.” The friend inside does not want to get up, but “at least because of his persistence he will get up and give him whatever he needs.” Then the Lord says plainly: “So I say to you, Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you.” And he ends: “If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” The greatest gift to ask for is the Holy Spirit, and the Church is now walking toward Pentecost. St Augustine said that God delays at times so that our desire may grow and become able to receive what he wants to give (in substance). Begin today to pray each day for the Holy Spirit, and keep knocking: for your family, for those who have fallen away, and for Christians who are persecuted today, as Mar Shemun's flock once was.
outline: Opening
Ask: have I grown since Easter, or settled down?
Point 1 · Go on toward perfection
A foundation is laid in order to build.
Point 2 · The ground that drinks the rain
Mar Shemun and the official who came back.
Point 3 · Ask, search, knock
The Father gives the Holy Spirit.
Take-home line
“Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you.”
live: Pray for the Spirit (Luke 11:13)
From today until Pentecost (16 May), pray every day: “Heavenly Father, give me your Holy Spirit.”
Pray for the persecuted
Remember by name one country where Christians suffer today, and pray for them this week.
2027-04-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you have poured the rain of your grace upon us this Easter. Do not let us settle down, but lead us on toward perfection, and make our lives produce a crop that is useful to others. By the prayers of Mar Shemun Bar Sabbae and the martyrs of Persia, give courage to all Christians who suffer for your name, and bring back those who have fallen away. Teach us to ask, to search and to knock, and fill us with the Holy Spirit whom the Father gives to those who ask him. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The Father who gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask sends the Spirit upon the bread and wine in the Holy Qurbono, making them the Body and Blood of the risen Lord; let us ask for the same Spirit for ourselves.

2027-04-15.title: Thursday after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: A priest through the power of an indestructible life
Strive to enter through the narrow door
2027-04-15.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Second Sunday after the Resurrection. The Letter to the Hebrews is read on most weekdays of these weeks.
2027-04-15.verse: One who has become a priest, not through a legal requirement concerning physical descent, but through the power of an indestructible life.
theo: Christ is risen! In these weeks of Qyomtho our Church reads the Letter to the Hebrews almost every weekday, and today it asks a bold question. Israel had a priesthood given by God himself: the sons of Aaron, from the tribe of Levi, served at the altar, and “the people received the law under this priesthood.” Why, then, did the Scriptures speak of “another priest arising according to the order of Melchizedek”? Jesus was not a Levite; “it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah.” His priesthood does not rest on a family tree. He became a priest “not through a legal requirement concerning physical descent, but through the power of an indestructible life.” This is an Easter sentence.
