The life that the Cross could not end and the tomb could not hold is the very foundation of his priesthood. The Letter does not despise the priesthood of Aaron; that priesthood was God's gift and a preparation, and the Church sees in it a figure of what Christ fulfils (Catechism 1539–1545). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, observes that a priest who dies needs a successor, but the priest who lives for ever needs none (in substance).

The Gospel finds Jesus on the road, “teaching as he made his way to Jerusalem.” Someone asks, “Lord, will only a few be saved?” Jesus does not give a number. He turns the question from curiosity to decision: “Strive to enter through the narrow door.” A day comes when the owner of the house has shut the door, and some will knock and say, “We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.” Having been near him is not yet the same as having entered by him. The warning is not for one people; it is for every believer who thinks that knowing the Lord's name or sitting at his table is a guarantee without a changed life, and so it speaks first to us who receive the Holy Qurbono. Christian writers have said that the door is narrow only for the proud; for the humble it is wide enough. Then comes the great hope of the passage: “people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.” We are among those who came from the east. The faith reached our shores through the preaching of the apostle Mar Thoma, as our tradition holds, and now we too are called to the banquet.

How do we live this today? The priest who lives for ever is the priest of every Holy Qurbono. When the celebrant stands at the altar of our church, it is Christ, risen and alive, who offers and who gives himself; “he always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). The “better hope, through which we approach God” is not an idea but a person. So come to the Holy Qurbono this Easter season with the readiness of one who enters a door, not only of one who watches from the street. Pray today for the priests of our eparchy and for those preparing for the priesthood, that they may serve as men who belong to the eternal priest. And choose the narrow door in small things: one honest word, one act of forgiveness, one confession made before the coming Sunday. The door is narrow because it is the shape of Christ himself, and through him the way is open to all.
outline: Opening
Ask: am I standing at the door, or have I entered?
Point 1 · A priest who cannot die
His priesthood rests on the power of an indestructible life.
Point 2 · The narrow door
Nearness is not yet entrance; humility makes the door wide.
Point 3 · From east and west
The banquet of the kingdom, and our place in it.
Take-home line
“Through the power of an indestructible life.”
live: Approach through him (Hebrews 7:19)
Before the Holy Qurbono this week, spend a minute in silence asking Christ the High Priest to bring you to the Father.
Strive to enter (Luke 13:24)
Choose one hard but right thing you have been postponing, and do it before Sunday.
2027-04-15.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you became our high priest through the power of an indestructible life. You live for ever to make intercession for us. Bring us through the narrow door of humility, that we may not only eat and drink in your presence but truly belong to you. Gather your children from east and west, from north and south, to the table of your kingdom, and keep our priests faithful to you. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At every Holy Qurbono the living Christ, priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, offers himself and gives us his Body and Blood, the bread and wine of the new and eternal covenant.

2027-04-16.title: Friday after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: The mediator of a new covenant; the blood of the covenant
Take the lowest place; invite the poor
2027-04-16.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Second Sunday after the Resurrection. On Fridays the Church remembers the Lord's Passion; in Qyomtho she remembers it in the light of the empty tomb.
2027-04-16.verse: For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.
theo: Christ is risen! On this Friday of the Easter season the Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the Lord's death, but as something that has already borne its fruit. Jesus “is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.” The Letter plays on a word that in Greek means both “covenant” and “will.” A will takes effect only when the one who made it has died; until then the heirs receive nothing. So with us: by his death on the Cross, Christ made the inheritance ours. Then the Letter recalls Mount Sinai, where Moses took the blood of the sacrifice, sprinkled the book and the people, and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that God has ordained for you.” In the Upper Room Jesus took the cup and used those very words of himself: “this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). And here is the wonder of Easter: in every other will the one who makes it stays dead. Our testator rose on the third day, and he himself now hands the inheritance to his heirs.

The Gospel takes us to a meal. Jesus is a guest in the house of a leader of the Pharisees, and he notices “how the guests chose the places of honor.” He tells them: “When you are invited... go and sit down at the lowest place, so that when your host comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’” This is more than good manners. It describes the way of Jesus himself, who “humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8), and whom the Father raised and exalted. “For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.” Then Jesus turns to his host: do not invite only those who can invite you back, but “invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you, for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” St John Chrysostom urged the families of Antioch to keep a room in their homes for Christ, that is, for the poor stranger, and to set a place for him at their table (in substance).

Notice the Easter word at the end of the Gospel: “the resurrection of the righteous.” Because Christ is risen, a kindness that is never returned on earth is not lost. It is stored up with God. Our Kerala celebrations know the struggle Jesus describes: the seating at a wedding, the chairs kept for important guests, the gift lists, the invitations sent with an eye to who will invite us back. This week, turn one of these customs around. Invite someone to your table who cannot repay you; give a gift that will not be recorded; at a function, take the lower chair gladly. And remember that at the Holy Qurbono every one of us is a guest who has been called up higher. We come not because we have earned the place, but because the host has said, “Friend, come.” The blood of the new covenant is given to sinners, and the inheritance is offered to all who are called.
outline: Opening
Ask: where do I sit when I am invited, and whom do I invite?
Point 1 · The blood of the new covenant
A will that the testator himself rose to carry out.
Point 2 · The lowest place
The way of Jesus, humbled and exalted.
Point 3 · Repaid at the resurrection
Generosity that waits for God's reward.
Take-home line
“You will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”
live: Take the lowest place (Luke 14:10)
At the next function or meeting you attend, choose a lower seat gladly and serve someone else first.
Invite those who cannot repay (Luke 14:13)
This week, share a meal or a packet of food with someone who has no way of returning it.
2027-04-16.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, mediator of the new covenant, by your death you made us heirs of the eternal inheritance, and by your Resurrection you live to give it to us. Teach us your humility, that we may take the lowest place without bitterness and rejoice when others are honoured. Open our hands and our homes to the poor, the sick and the lonely, who cannot repay us, and keep our hope fixed on the resurrection of the righteous. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the Blood of the new covenant, poured out once on the Cross, is truly given to us for the forgiveness of sins, and the risen Lord calls each of us, unworthy guests, to come up higher to his table.

2027-04-17.title: Saturday after the Second Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified
The great dinner: “Come; for everything is ready now”
2027-04-17.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Second Sunday after the Resurrection. This evening the Third Sunday after the Resurrection begins with Evening Prayer; its Evening Gospel is Mark 16:9–13.
2027-04-17.verse: For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified.
theo: Christ is risen! The Letter to the Hebrews sets two pictures side by side. In the first, “every priest stands day after day at his service, offering again and again the same sacrifices that can never take away sins.” In the second, Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” and “sat down at the right hand of God.” The priests of the old covenant stand, because their work is never finished. Christ sits, because his work is done: he died once, rose, and is enthroned with the Father. “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified.” What, then, do we do at every Holy Qurbono? We do not add a new sacrifice to the Cross, and we do not repeat it as if it were incomplete. The one sacrifice of Calvary is made present on our altar, and the risen Lord who offered it once offers himself now through the ministry of the priest (Catechism 1366–1367). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, put it simply: we do not offer one lamb today and another tomorrow, but always the same; the sacrifice is one (in substance).

The Letter then calls the Holy Spirit as witness, quoting the prophet Jeremiah: “I will put my laws in their hearts, and I will write them on their minds,” and “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” This is the new covenant: not a law carved on stone outside us, but the Spirit writing God's will inside us, and a forgiveness so complete that God himself chooses not to remember. The Gospel then opens a door to the feast. At a dinner someone exclaims, “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” Jesus answers with a parable. A man gave a great dinner and sent his servant to say, “Come; for everything is ready now.” But they all began to make excuses: a field, five yoke of oxen, a new marriage. None of these is a sin. They are good things put in the place of the invitation. The parable is not aimed at one people; the first disciples who accepted the invitation were themselves sons and daughters of Israel. It is a warning to every invited guest, and so to us. St Gregory the Great observed that the pleasures of the body, once possessed, soon weary us, but spiritual delights, once tasted, make us hungry for more (in substance).

The master then sends his servant into the streets and lanes for “the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame,” and again to the roads and lanes: “compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.” The Church reads this “compel” as the urgency of love, never as force, for the act of faith must be given willingly (Catechism 160; Dignitatis Humanae 10). Tonight, as Saturday evening opens the Lord's Day, the invitation comes to us again: “Come; for everything is ready now.” Everything is ready at the Holy Qurbono tomorrow: the Word, the Body and Blood of the Lord, the peace of the risen Christ. What excuse is waiting in my week? A tuition class, a function, a site visit, tiredness? Prepare tonight. Make peace with someone, go to confession if you need to, plan to go as a family, and bring along one person who has stopped coming. The house is not yet full; there is still room.
outline: Opening
Ask: what excuse have I given God most often?
Point 1 · One sacrifice, for all time
The priests stand; Christ sits at the right hand.
Point 2 · Written on hearts, remembered no more
The new covenant of the Spirit and of forgiveness.
Point 3 · “Come; for everything is ready now”
The great dinner, the excuses, and the house still to be filled.
Take-home line
“By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified.”
live: Answer the invitation (Luke 14:17)
Plan tonight how your whole family will reach the Holy Qurbono tomorrow, and remove one excuse in advance.
There is still room (Luke 14:22)
Invite one person to come with you to church this Sunday, and offer to bring them.
2027-04-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, by one offering you have perfected for all time those who are sanctified, and now you sit at the right hand of the Father. Write your law on our hearts and remember our sins no more. You have prepared a great dinner and say to us, “Come; for everything is ready now.” Deliver us from every excuse that keeps us from your table, and send us into the streets and lanes to bring others with us, until your house is filled. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbono is not a new sacrifice but the one sacrifice of the Cross made present, in which the risen Christ gives us his true Body and Blood; here the great dinner of the kingdom is already set before us.

2027-04-19.title: Monday after the Third Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: A new and living way through the curtain; do not neglect to meet together
The shepherd who goes after the one lost sheep
2027-04-19.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Third Sunday after the Resurrection. Yesterday the Church heard of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus.
2027-04-19.verse: Let us hold fast to the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who has promised is faithful.
theo: Christ is risen! Yesterday we walked with the two disciples to Emmaus and saw them run back to Jerusalem to find the others. Today the Letter to the Hebrews tells us what the risen Lord has opened for us: “we have confidence to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain (that is, through his flesh).” In the temple at Jerusalem a curtain separated the Holy of Holies, and only the high priest passed through it, once a year. When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). His own flesh, given on the Cross and raised on the third day, has become the doorway into the presence of God. In our churches the curtain of the sanctuary is drawn back as the Holy Qurbono begins, and the faithful see the altar opened before them. We may see in it a sign of what Christ has done: heaven is no longer closed. So the Letter invites us: “let us approach with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water,” words that recall our Baptism.

Then come three simple commands. “Let us hold fast to the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who has promised is faithful.” “Let us consider how to provoke one another to love and good deeds.” And: do not neglect “to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another.” Already in the first generation some Christians were drifting away from the Sunday assembly. The Gospel shows the heart of God for those who drift. Tax collectors and sinners are “coming near to listen” to Jesus, and some Pharisees and scribes grumble: “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.” They were devout people, and their grumbling is a temptation that every religious person knows. Jesus answers with a story: a shepherd with a hundred sheep loses one, leaves the ninety-nine, goes “after the one that is lost until he finds it,” lays it on his shoulders, and calls his neighbours to rejoice. St Ambrose saw in the shepherd's shoulders the arms of the Cross, on which Christ carried our sins home (in substance).

Put the two readings together and a task appears. The new and living way is open; the shepherd is searching; and we are asked not to neglect meeting together, but to encourage one another. Who is missing from our Sunday Qurbono? Perhaps a young person who moved to a city for studies, a family hurt by some quarrel in the parish, an elderly person no longer able to walk to church, a neighbour who simply lost the habit. This week, be the shepherd's hands. Call one of them, visit, offer a ride, carry the Holy Qurbono's joy to those who cannot come by asking the priest to bring Holy Communion to the sick. And look into your own heart: if you are the one who has wandered, the Lord is not waiting at a distance to scold you. He is already on the road looking for you, and there is joy in heaven when you are found.
outline: Opening
Ask: who is missing from our Sunday assembly, and who is looking for them?
Point 1 · A new and living way
Through the curtain of his flesh, heaven is opened.
Point 2 · Do not neglect to meet together
Hold fast, provoke one another to love, encourage one another.
Point 3 · The shepherd who searches
Until he finds it, and joy in heaven.
Take-home line
“He who has promised is faithful.”
live: Encourage one another (Hebrews 10:25)
Phone or visit one person who has stopped coming to the Holy Qurbono, simply to tell them they are missed.
Rejoice with me (Luke 15:6)
When someone returns to church or to the sacraments, welcome them warmly and without comment on the past.
2027-04-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen Shepherd, you opened for us a new and living way through the curtain of your flesh, and you go after every sheep that is lost until you find it. Give us a true heart and full assurance of faith. Keep us faithful to the confession of our hope, and make us eager to meet together, to provoke one another to love and good deeds, and to go out to those who have wandered. Carry home on your shoulders all who are lost, and fill heaven with joy. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: Through the flesh of Christ, torn on the Cross and risen in glory, the way into the sanctuary is open; at the Holy Qurbono we approach that sanctuary and receive his true Body and Blood.

2027-04-20.title: Tuesday after the Third Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: Do not spurn the blood of the covenant
You cannot serve God and wealth; what God has joined
2027-04-20.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Third Sunday after the Resurrection.
2027-04-20.verse: No slave can serve two masters; for a slave will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.
theo: Christ is risen! Today's Gospel is plain speech about money. “If then you have not been faithful with the dishonest wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches?” Then the sentence everyone remembers: “No slave can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and wealth.” Jesus does not say that money is evil; he says it makes a poor master. Wealth asks for the whole heart, and so does God; one of them must give way. Luke adds that some who heard this “were lovers of money” and ridiculed him, and Jesus answers: “God knows your hearts; for what is prized by human beings is an abomination in the sight of God.” The warning is for every listener in every age, and the Catechism repeats the bold words of St John Chrysostom: not to let the poor share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life; the goods we possess are not ours, but theirs (Catechism 2446). The risen Lord does not ask us to despise the world; he asks us to use what passes so as to gain what lasts.

Then Jesus speaks of the law: “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one stroke of a letter in the law to be dropped,” and he gives one example where he restores God's first plan: “Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery.” Jesus takes marriage back to the beginning, when God made man and woman to become “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). The Church holds that a valid, consummated marriage between baptized persons cannot be dissolved by any human power (Catechism 1614–1615, 2382). This teaching is a word of protection, especially for wives who in the ancient world could be sent away with a single document. It is never a reason to treat with coldness those whose marriages have broken down. Many were abandoned against their will; many carry wounds. The Church is asked to accompany them with patience and love, to help them examine their situation in truth, and to keep them close to the life of the parish (Pope Francis, Amoris Laetitia, 2016).

The Letter to the Hebrews today sounds severe: “if we willfully persist in sin after having received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,” and “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” What does it mean? The Letter has spent chapters showing that Christ's one sacrifice is the only sacrifice for sin. Whoever deliberately rejects it, trampling on “the Son of God” and outraging “the Spirit of grace,” turns away from the only remedy there is. In the third century some, like the followers of Novatian, read these lines as if the Church could never forgive grave sin after Baptism. The Church rejected that reading and kept the door of Penance open: there is no offence, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive (Catechism 982). On the very evening of his Resurrection the Lord breathed on the apostles and gave them power to forgive sins (John 20:22–23). The fearful thing is not the hand of God but refusing it. King David once chose: “let us fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy is great” (2 Samuel 24:14). Let that be our choice too, in the confessional this Easter.
outline: Opening
Ask: who is really the master of my money, my time and my heart?
Point 1 · God or wealth
Money is a useful servant and a poor master.
Point 2 · What God has joined
Marriage restored to the beginning, and the Church's care for the wounded.
Point 3 · The hands of the living God
A severe warning, and the open door of mercy.
Take-home line
“You cannot serve God and wealth.”
live: Be faithful with little (Luke 16:10–11)
Look at last month's spending and set aside a fixed share for the poor before anything else.
Choose the hand of the Lord (Hebrews 10:31)
If you have been staying away from confession, go this week; the door is open.
2027-04-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you alone are our Master. Deliver us from the love of money and teach us to use the goods of this world in faithfulness and generosity. Bless husbands and wives with faithful love, and surround with your compassion those whose marriages have been broken. Keep us from ever spurning the blood of the covenant, and when we fall, bring us back to the mercy you gave your Church on the evening of your Resurrection. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Blood of the covenant by which we were sanctified is truly given to us; to receive it with faith is to choose the merciful hand of the living God.

2027-04-21.title: Wednesday after the Third Sunday after Qyomtho
readings: Recall the days after you were enlightened; do not abandon your confidence
2027-04-21.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Third Sunday after the Resurrection.
2027-04-21.verse: Do not, therefore, abandon that confidence of yours; it brings a great reward.
theo: Christ is risen! The Letter to the Hebrews asks its readers to remember: “recall those earlier days when, after you had been enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings.” The early Christians often called Baptism “enlightenment.” St Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, explains that the washing of Baptism is called illumination, because those who receive it are enlightened in their understanding (First Apology 61). In the Easter season the Church thinks especially of those baptized at Easter, and of our own Baptism. The first readers of this Letter had paid a price for that light. They had been “publicly exposed to abuse and persecution”; they had stood by others who suffered; they “had compassion for those who were in prison,” and they “cheerfully accepted the plundering” of their possessions, “knowing that you yourselves possessed something better and more lasting.” Now, years later, some were growing tired. So the Letter says: “Do not, therefore, abandon that confidence of yours; it brings a great reward. For you need endurance.”

The risen Lord is our reason for endurance. “In a very little while, the one who is coming will come and will not delay; but my righteous one will live by faith.” The Letter ends the passage with a sentence of courage: “we are not among those who shrink back and so are lost, but among those who have faith and so are saved.” In the Gospel Jesus shows that faith is needed not only under persecution but in the daily life of the community. “Occasions for stumbling are bound to come, but woe to anyone by whom they come!” He speaks with great seriousness about anyone who causes “one of these little ones to stumble,” words that the Church today hears as a solemn call to protect children and the vulnerable in every parish and home. Then he asks for something that seems impossible: “if the same person sins against you seven times a day, and turns back to you seven times and says, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive.” The apostles' reply is honest: “Increase our faith!” They understood that only faith can forgive like that.

Jesus answers: “If you had faith the size of a mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.” The mulberry tree had deep and stubborn roots, like a resentment that has grown in us for years. A small faith in the risen Lord can uproot it. How do we live this today? First, remember your own enlightenment: take out your baptismal certificate, find the date, and thank God for the light you received. Second, look for one person whom you have stopped forgiving, perhaps someone who keeps hurting you in the same way, and ask the Lord for faith enough to forgive once more, while also asking wisely for the change that true repentance requires. Third, be a guardian of the little ones: let no word or example of yours make a child stumble. And when you feel tired in faith, make the apostles' prayer your own, especially before the Holy Qurbono: “Lord, increase our faith.”
outline: Opening
Ask: when did I last thank God for my Baptism?
Point 1 · Do not abandon your confidence
Remember the light you received, and endure.
Point 2 · Forgive seven times
Protect the little ones, rebuke in love, forgive again.
Point 3 · Increase our faith
A mustard seed of faith that uproots the mulberry tree.
Take-home line
“Do not, therefore, abandon that confidence of yours.”
live: Recall the earlier days (Hebrews 10:32)
Find the date of your Baptism, and on that day each year go to the Holy Qurbono in thanksgiving.
Forgive again (Luke 17:4)
Name one person you have stopped forgiving, and pray for them by name every day this week.
2027-04-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you enlightened us in Baptism and called us to share in your victory. When we grow tired, do not let us abandon our confidence; give us endurance to do the will of God and receive what you have promised. Make us guardians of the little ones, and give us hearts that forgive again and again. Increase our faith, that even a mustard seed of it may uproot the bitterness that has grown in us. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the One who is coming already comes to us, truly present in his Body and Blood, to strengthen the faith of the enlightened and give us endurance.

2027-04-22.title: Thursday of the third week after Qyomtho
readings: Surrounded by a cloud of witnesses, looking to Jesus
The widow and the unjust judge: pray always and do not lose heart
2027-04-22.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Third Sunday after Qyomtho.
2027-04-22.verse: let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus the pioneer and perfecter of our faith
theo: Three and a half weeks after Qyomtho, the joy of Easter has to learn to walk. The first rush of the feast is over; ordinary days have come back, with work, exams, illness and bills. The Letter to the Hebrews speaks to exactly this moment. It has just finished its long roll-call of the faithful of old, Abel and Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Moses and Rahab and the prophets, and now it turns to us: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us.” The picture is a stadium. The runners are on the track, and the stands are full of those who have already finished. St John Chrysostom pictures the saints as spectators who once ran the same course and now cheer us on, so that we may not be ashamed to slacken before such a crowd (Homilies on Hebrews 28, in substance). In the Holy Qurbono our Church names them every time: the Mother of God, the prophets and apostles, the martyrs and confessors, the holy fathers and all the faithful departed. We never run alone.

But the runner does not keep looking at the stands. Hebrews tells us where to fix our eyes: “looking to Jesus the pioneer and perfecter of our faith, who for the sake of the joy that was set before him endured the cross, disregarding its shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God.” Jesus is the pioneer, the one who has already run the whole course, through the Cross and the tomb, and has broken the tape on Easter morning. He is also the perfecter: he will bring our faltering faith to its finish. “Consider him who endured such hostility against himself from sinners, so that you may not grow weary or lose heart.” The Gospel takes up the same danger of losing heart. “Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.” A widow, with no money, no husband and no influence, keeps coming to a judge “who neither feared God nor had respect for people,” saying, “Grant me justice against my opponent.” In the end he gives in, only to be rid of her. Then the Lord draws the lesson from the lesser to the greater: if even this judge yields, “will not God grant justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night?” God is not the unjust judge; he is the Father. The point of the parable is not that we must wear God down, but that we must not let ourselves be worn down. St Augustine wrote to the widow Proba that to pray always is to keep desire for God alive in the heart without ceasing, and that our set times of prayer rekindle that desire when it cools (Letter 130, in substance).

Our Church gives us a rhythm for this persevering prayer: the seven times of prayer of the Shehimo, from the Evening prayer through the night to the Ninth Hour, so that the whole day is carried to God. Few families can pray all seven, but every family can keep two: the evening prayer together before supper and a short prayer on waking. Jesus ends the parable with a question that is meant for each of us: “And yet, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” Faith is found in people who keep running and keep asking. If there is a prayer you stopped making because nothing seemed to happen, a child far from the Church, a marriage under strain, a healing not yet given, take it up again today. Bring it to the Holy Qurbono, where the risen Lord who finished the race gives himself as food for runners who are tired. And remember the cloud of witnesses: ask one saint you love to run beside you this week.
outline: Opening
Ask: what prayer have I quietly stopped praying because I lost heart?
Point 1 · A great cloud of witnesses
The stadium full of those who finished the race.
Point 2 · Looking to Jesus
The pioneer who ran through the Cross to the joy beyond it.
Point 3 · Pray always and do not lose heart
The widow who kept coming, and the Father who hears.
Take-home line
“Let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us.”
live: Take up the dropped prayer (Luke 18:1)
Write down one intention you stopped praying for, and pray for it every evening until Sunday.
Lay aside every weight (Hebrews 12:1)
Name one habit that slows you down in following Jesus and leave it aside for one week.
2027-04-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, pioneer and perfecter of our faith, for the joy set before you you endured the Cross and now you are seated at the right hand of the Father. Keep our eyes fixed on you. Surrounded by the cloud of witnesses, by your holy Mother and all the saints, help us to lay aside every weight and the sin that clings to us, and to run with perseverance. Teach us to pray always and not to lose heart, trusting that the Father hears the cry of his children day and night. When you come, may you find faith in us. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the runner who has finished the course feeds those still on the track: in the Holy Qurbono the risen Jesus gives his own Body and Blood as strength for the race.

2027-04-23.title: Mar Geevarghese Sahada · St George the Great Martyr · Friday of the third week after Qyomtho
readings: Share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus
Sheep in the midst of wolves; the one who endures to the end will be saved
2027-04-23.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Third Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the feast of Mar Geevarghese Sahada, St George the Martyr.
2027-04-23.verse: Share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
theo: There is hardly a Christian village in Kerala without a Geevarghese, a Varghese or a George. The name of today's saint has passed from Syriac (Giwargis) into Malayalam homes, and his image, a young soldier on a white horse with his lance aimed at the dragon, hangs in churches of every tradition among us. Today our Church keeps his feast. What history can say with confidence is short and strong. George was a Christian soldier who gave his life for Christ in the great persecution of the early fourth century, most likely under the emperor Diocletian, and his tomb at Lydda (Diospolis) in Palestine was a place of pilgrimage within a few generations. The longer stories of his trials grew up later; the Church has always honoured him above all as a witness. Our tradition calls him Sahada, the Syriac word for martyr, which means witness. A decree attributed to Pope Gelasius I placed him among those whose names are rightly revered among people but whose deeds are known fully only to God (in substance). That is enough. We do not need every detail of his story to know what he did: when the empire demanded that he deny Christ, he chose Christ.

The readings show why a soldier became the image of every Christian. St Paul writes to Timothy: “You then, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus... Share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving in the army gets entangled in everyday affairs; the soldier's aim is to please the enlisting officer.” Paul adds the athlete, who is not crowned “without competing according to the rules,” and the farmer “who does the work.” All three are pictures of steady, faithful labour, not of sudden heroics. George's martyrdom did not come from nowhere; it grew out of a soldier's daily faithfulness to the one who had enlisted him in Baptism. St Ignatius of Antioch, himself on the way to martyrdom, wrote to Polycarp: please the one under whom you serve as soldiers; let none of you be found a deserter; let your Baptism be your shield, your faith your helmet, your love your spear, your endurance your armour (Letter to Polycarp 6, in substance). In the Gospel Jesus sends his disciples out with no illusions: “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” They will be handed over and “dragged before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and the Gentiles.” And he adds the promise that every martyr has leaned on: “do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say... for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” Finally: “the one who endures to the end will be saved.”

Why does a martyr's feast belong in the season of Qyomtho? Because martyrs are the strongest proof that Christians really believe in the Resurrection. No one dies for a story he suspects to be false. St Augustine taught that it is not the suffering but the cause that makes a martyr (Letter 89, in substance): George is honoured not because he was tortured, but because he would not betray the risen Lord. The famous dragon is a later legend, best read as a picture: the dragon is the old enemy, and every Christian who refuses evil for Christ's sake strikes at it. In our own time Christians are still dragged before councils, in many lands, for the name of Jesus. Pray for them today. And ask yourself where your own small martyrdom lies: in refusing a bribe at the office, in telling the truth at home when a lie would be easier, in keeping Sunday when the world pulls the other way. Take part in the Holy Qurbono for the feast if you can, and if you bear his name, thank God for it and ask for his courage.
conn: A soldier of Christ.
2 Timothy 2:3–4 and the life of St George: the soldier who pleased the one who enlisted him, even at the cost of his life.
Sheep among wolves.
Matthew 10:16–22: Jesus foretold that his witnesses would be handed over to governors; the martyrs are the fulfilment of his word and of his promise that the Spirit would speak through them.
Martyr means witness.
Hebrews 12:1, read yesterday, speaks of a cloud of witnesses; today the Church honours one of them by the Syriac title Sahada.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch

Please the one under whom you serve as soldiers; let none of you be found a deserter. Let your Baptism be your shield, your faith your helmet, your love your spear, your endurance your armour (Letter to Polycarp 6, in substance).
St Augustine
It is not the punishment that makes a true martyr, but the cause for which he suffers (Letter 89, in substance).
magis: Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity.
Catechism 2474
The Church has gathered with great care the records of those who persevered to the end in witnessing to their faith: these are the acts of the martyrs.

outline: Opening
Ask: what does it cost me today to be known as a Christian?
Point 1 · A good soldier of Christ Jesus
Daily faithfulness to the one who enlisted us in Baptism.
Point 2 · Sheep among wolves
The Spirit speaks through those who are handed over.
Point 3 · Sahada: a witness to the risen Lord
Why the martyrs belong to Easter.

“Share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus.”
live: Pray for the persecuted (Matthew 10:17–18)
Pray today for Christians who are on trial, in prison or in danger for the name of Jesus.
One faithful refusal (2 Timothy 2:4)
Choose one place this week where you will refuse something wrong, quietly and firmly, for Christ's sake.
2027-04-23.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you gave Mar Geevarghese the courage of a good soldier and the crown of a martyr. You sent your disciples as sheep among wolves and promised that your Spirit would speak through them. By his prayers make us strong in your grace; let us not be entangled in what is passing, but seek only to please you who enlisted us in Baptism. Strengthen all Christians who suffer for your name, and give us endurance to the end, so that with all your witnesses we may share in your Resurrection. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The martyrs drew their strength from the altar: in the Holy Qurbono the Lord who laid down his life and rose again gives himself to us, the bread of those who bear witness.

2027-04-24.title: Saturday of the third week after Qyomtho
readings: The Lord disciplines those whom he loves; pursue peace and holiness
The Pharisee and the tax collector: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”
2027-04-24.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Third Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam prints the Epistle as “Hebrews 12:1-4–17.” Since Thursday already read Hebrews 12:1–3, it is read here as Hebrews 12:4–17; by the same kind of misprint it could also mean Hebrews 12:14–17, which lies within this reading. Please verify locally.
2027-04-24.verse: But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even look up to heaven, but was beating his breast and saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
theo: Two men go up to the temple to pray, and Jesus lets us listen to both. The Pharisee, “standing by himself, was praying thus, ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people: thieves, rogues, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of all my income.’” Every word of his list may be true. He really fasts; he really gives. What is wrong is the direction of his gaze: he looks at himself, and then sideways at the tax collector, and hardly at God at all. Luke tells us at the start whom the parable is for: “some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded others with contempt.” The tax collector, “standing far off, would not even look up to heaven, but was beating his breast and saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’” He has no list. He has only a need, and he names it. And Jesus gives the verdict: “this man went down to his home justified rather than the other; for all who exalt themselves will be humbled, but all who humble themselves will be exalted.” St Augustine said the Pharisee came to the Physician and showed him only his healthy limbs, while the tax collector uncovered his wounds, and so only he was healed (in substance).

The Letter to the Hebrews shows what God does with the humble. It begins with a sober line that follows on from yesterday's feast of a martyr: “In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.” Then it speaks of discipline, quoting Proverbs: “My child, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, or lose heart when you are punished by him; for the Lord disciplines those whom he loves.” God corrects us not as an angry master but as a father: “he disciplines us for our good, in order that we may share his holiness.” It hurts at the time, Hebrews admits honestly, “but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” So “lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees.” The reading then gives three warnings. “Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.” Watch “that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble.” And do not become like Esau, “who sold his birthright for a single meal.” The tax collector let God's discipline reach him, and it healed him. The Pharisee had no room for it; he had already passed judgment on himself and on his neighbour.

Our Church gives us the tax collector's prayer on our lips again and again. In the Holy Qurbono and in every hour of the Shehimo we sing “Kurielaison,” Lord, have mercy, and we bow and make the sign of the Cross. These are not empty repetitions; they are the tax collector beating his breast. This Saturday, as the week ends, is a good day to prepare for Sunday by making a good confession, or at least an honest examination of conscience. Ask yourself the Pharisee's question in reverse: not “how am I better than others?” but “where do I need God's mercy?” Is there a root of bitterness in your family, an old quarrel that keeps sending up shoots? Pursue peace: make one call, send one message, offer one word of reconciliation before you go to the Qurbono tomorrow. The risen Lord, who showed his wounds to Thomas, is not ashamed of ours.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I pray, do I look at God, at myself, or at others?
Point 1 · Two men went up to pray
The list of the Pharisee and the need of the tax collector.
Point 2 · The discipline of a Father
Correction that makes us share his holiness.
Point 3 · Pursue peace and holiness
Roots of bitterness and the birthright we must not sell.
Take-home line
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”
live: Pray the tax collector's prayer (Luke 18:13)
Several times today, quietly, pray: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.
Pull up one root of bitterness (Hebrews 12:15)
Before Sunday's Qurbono, make one step of reconciliation with someone you are at odds with.
2027-04-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you rose from the dead and showed your wounds to your disciples. Deliver us from the pride that trusts in itself and looks down on others. Give us the humility of the tax collector, who stood far off and asked only for mercy. When the Father disciplines us, let us not lose heart, but receive it as the love that makes us share his holiness. Pull up every root of bitterness in our hearts and homes, help us to pursue peace with everyone, and bring us to see your face. Lord, have mercy on us. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: Before we approach the altar we say with the tax collector, Lord, have mercy; and the Lord who justifies the humble gives himself to us in the Holy Qurbono, healing the wounds we show him.

2027-04-26.title: Monday of the fourth week after Qyomtho
readings: You have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant
The parable of the sower: “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
2027-04-26.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho.
2027-04-26.verse: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering
theo: Yesterday the Church remembered St Mark the Evangelist, and today, fittingly, the Gospel comes from his book. Jesus is teaching by the Sea of Galilee, and the crowd is so large that “he got into a boat on the sea and sat there, while the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land.” The boat becomes a pulpit. And his first word is a command: “Listen!” Then comes a story every farmer in Kerala would understand. “A sower went out to sow.” Some seed falls on the path and the birds eat it; some on rocky ground, where it springs up quickly but withers in the sun “since it had no root”; some among thorns, which choke it; and some “into good soil and brought forth grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.” The sower is generous to the point of seeming careless: he throws seed everywhere, even where it may not grow. So God scatters his word on every heart, never first asking whether we deserve it. The question the parable leaves with us is not about the sower, nor about the seed, which is always good, but about the soil. St Ephrem the Syrian, our own teacher in the Syriac tradition, marvelled that no one can grasp even one word of the Lord fully: we are like the thirsty who drink from a spring, and what we leave behind is far more than what we take (Commentary on the Diatessaron 1, in substance).

The Letter to the Hebrews tells us where that word is spoken most solemnly: in the worship of the Church. It sets two mountains side by side. The first is Sinai, where Israel received the Law: “a blazing fire, and darkness, and gloom, and a tempest, and the sound of a trumpet, and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that not another word be spoken to them.” Even Moses said, “I tremble with fear.” The second mountain is the one we have come to: “But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.” This is a picture of the Holy Qurbono. When our Church celebrates the holy mysteries, the veil is drawn back and we stand with the angels and the saints, singing with the Seraphim, “Holy, holy, holy.” The blood of Abel cried out from the ground for vengeance; the blood of Jesus, offered on the Cross and made present on the altar, speaks a better word: mercy, forgiveness, peace.

Put the two readings together and a practical question appears: what kind of soil do we bring to the Qurbono? Some of us arrive like the path, trampled by a hurried week, and the word is gone before we reach the door. Some are like the rocky ground: moved for a moment by a good homily, but with no root of daily prayer. Many are like the thorny ground: we hear, but the worries of money, exams, health and phones grow up around the word and choke it. The remedy is simple and old. Come a few minutes early and be still. Read the Sunday Gospel at home on Saturday night. After the Qurbono, keep one sentence from the readings and repeat it through the week. In this Qyomtho season the risen Lord is still walking beside us and opening the Scriptures, as he did on the road to Emmaus. Give him good soil, and he promises a harvest: thirty, sixty and a hundredfold.
outline: Opening
Ask: what happened to the last homily I heard? Where is that seed now?
Point 1 · A sower went out to sow
God scatters his word on every heart.
Point 2 · Not Sinai, but Zion
At the Qurbono we come to the festal gathering of heaven.
Point 3 · Good soil
Path, rock, thorns, and the heart that bears fruit.
Take-home line
“Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
live: Prepare the soil (Mark 4:8)
This week read next Sunday's Gospel at home the evening before, and come to the Qurbono five minutes early to be still.
Keep one word (Mark 4:9)
Choose one sentence from today's readings, write it on a card and read it every morning this week.
2027-04-26.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, sower of the word of life, you scatter your seed generously on every heart. Break up the hard paths of our hurry, give root to our good intentions, and pull out the thorns of worry that choke your word. Make us good soil, that we may bear fruit thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. You have brought us not to a mountain of fear but to Mount Zion, to the angels in festal gathering and to your sprinkled blood that speaks of mercy. Let us stand in awe and joy at your holy Qurbono. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At every Holy Qurbono we come to Mount Zion: with the angels and the saints we stand before Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, and receive his Body and the Blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

2027-04-27.title: Tuesday of the fourth week after Qyomtho · St Cletus, Pope
readings: A kingdom that cannot be shaken
The rich ruler; “we have left our homes and followed you”
2027-04-27.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam remembers St Cletus, Bishop of Rome.
2027-04-27.verse: Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us give thanks, by which we offer to God an acceptable worship with reverence and awe
theo: Kerala knows what it is for the ground to shake. Many of us remember the floods of 2018, when houses built over a lifetime were gone in a night and families learned how little of what they owned could really be kept. The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of a greater shaking. God's voice once “shook the earth” at Sinai, “but now he has promised, ‘Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven.’” This phrase, Hebrews explains, “indicates the removal of what is shaken... so that what cannot be shaken may remain.” Everything made will one day be tested. And then comes the good news: “Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us give thanks, by which we offer to God an acceptable worship with reverence and awe; for indeed our God is a consuming fire.” The kingdom of the risen Christ is the one thing that will not be washed away. The fitting response is thanksgiving and worship, which is exactly what the Holy Qurbono is: the great thanksgiving of the Church. But Hebrews also warns: “See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking.” God still speaks, from heaven, through his Son.

The Gospel shows a man who heard that voice and could not let go of what shakes. “A certain ruler asked him, ‘Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?’” He has kept the commandments since his youth, and he is sincere. Then Jesus says: “There is still one thing lacking. Sell all that you own and distribute the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” Luke records simply: “he became sad; for he was very rich.” He was holding on to the house that the flood would take. Jesus looks at him, not with anger but with sorrow, and says: “How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” The listeners ask, “Then who can be saved?” and he answers, “What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.” Then Peter speaks for the Twelve: “Look, we have left our homes and followed you.” Jesus' reply is one of the most generous promises in the Gospel: “there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not get back very much more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life.” What we let go of for Christ is not lost; it is placed in the one kingdom that cannot be shaken.

Today the Panchangam remembers St Cletus, one of the first Bishops of Rome after St Peter. St Irenaeus of Lyons, writing in the second century, lists the succession at Rome: after the apostles Peter and Paul came Linus, then Anencletus (Cletus), then Clement (Against Heresies III.3, in substance). Later tradition counts Cletus among the martyrs. We know very little more about him, but what we know is precious: he received what Peter had handed on and passed it on faithfully. He belongs to the unshakable kingdom because he built on the rock. Our own Church, since the reunion of 1930, lives in full communion with the Successor of Peter, and so we honour the early Bishops of Rome as fathers in the faith. Today, pray for the Pope and for our Major Archbishop-Catholicos and our bishops. And look at your own life after the readings: what are you holding on to that could be shaken away in a night? Let go of one thing this week, give something to the poor, and offer thanks at the Qurbono for the kingdom you are already receiving.
outline: Opening
Ask: if everything I own were washed away tonight, what would remain?
Point 1 · A kingdom that cannot be shaken
What shakes, what remains, and the worship of thanksgiving.
Point 2 · One thing lacking
The rich ruler and the treasure he could not let go.
Point 3 · We have left our homes
Peter's question, Christ's promise, and St Cletus who built on the rock.
Take-home line
“We are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.”
live: Let go of one thing (Luke 18:22)
Give away this week one thing you are attached to, to someone who needs it.
Give thanks (Hebrews 12:28)
At your next Qurbono, offer one specific thanksgiving to God for a gift that cannot be taken away.
2027-04-27.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you give us a kingdom that cannot be shaken. When the earth and the heavens are shaken, you remain. Deliver us from clinging to what passes, as the rich ruler clung to his wealth, and give us the courage of Peter and the apostles who left everything to follow you. By the prayers of St Cletus, who received the faith from your apostle Peter and handed it on faithfully, keep your Church firm on the rock, and bless our Holy Father the Pope and the bishops of our Church. Let us offer you, with reverence and awe, the worship of thanksgiving. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbono is the thanksgiving of those who are receiving an unshakable kingdom: on the altar the Lord gives us his Body and Blood, the treasure in heaven already given on earth.

2027-04-28.title: Wednesday of the fourth week after Qyomtho · Memory of Most Rev. Isaac Mar Yoohanon
readings: Remember your leaders; Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever
2027-04-28.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps the memory of Most Rev. Isaac Mar Yoohanon (1987) and gives John 10:11–18, John 14:1–6 or John 15:9–17 as alternative Gospels.
2027-04-28.verse: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
theo: Today the Panchangam asks us to remember Most Rev. Isaac Mar Yoohanon, a bishop of our Church, who entered his rest in 1987. Forty years have passed, and many younger members of our Church will not know his face. The Letter to the Hebrews tells us why such remembering matters: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.” The Church is not a club that begins again with each generation. It is a family with a memory. We received the faith from people who were baptized, taught, ordained and consecrated before us; they carried it through difficult years and handed it on. To remember them is to give thanks for them, to learn from them, and to pray for them. The Catholic Church has always prayed for her departed shepherds, asking that any stain of human weakness be washed away and that they may see the face of the Chief Shepherd. Then comes the line that holds all generations together: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” Bishops come and go; the Lord they served does not change. The Christ who called Mar Yoohanon is the Christ who calls us.

Hebrews goes on to the heart of the bishop's service and of the whole Church's life: “We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.” Christians are not people without a sacrifice. Our altar is the altar of the Holy Qurbono, where the one sacrifice of Christ on Calvary is made present and his true Body and Blood are given as food. Hebrews explains with an image from the old temple: the bodies of the sacrificed animals were burned outside the camp, and “Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood. Let us then go to him outside the camp and bear the abuse he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.” Two more sacrifices flow from the altar into daily life: “let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name,” and “Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.” Worship, praise and sharing belong together. St Augustine once told his people: for you I am a bishop, with you I am a Christian; the first is a burden, the second a grace (Sermon 340, in substance).

The Gospel gives the measure of every shepherd and every steward. “Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time? Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.” A bishop gives the household its food: the word of God, the sacraments, wise guidance. But every Christian is a steward of something: parents of their children, teachers of their pupils, employers of their workers, the healthy of the sick who depend on them. The warning is sharp: the wicked servant who says “My master is delayed” and begins to beat his fellow servants and to drink with drunkards will be surprised by the master's return. Our Lord rose and ascended and will come again; we do not know the hour. Today, pray for the soul of Mar Yoohanon and for all the bishops and priests who served our Church and have gone before us. Pray for our present bishops. And ask yourself: in the household entrusted to me, am I giving food at the proper time?
outline: Opening
Ask: who first spoke the word of God to me, and have I thanked God for them?
Point 1 · Remember your leaders
The Church as a family with a memory; praying for our departed shepherds.
Point 2 · We have an altar
The sacrifice of Christ, the sacrifice of praise and the sacrifice of sharing.
Point 3 · The faithful and wise servant
Every Christian a steward; food at the proper time.
Take-home line
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
live: Remember and pray (Hebrews 13:7)
Pray today for the soul of Mar Yoohanon and of one priest or catechist who taught you the faith and has died.
Food at the proper time (Matthew 24:45)
Think of one person who depends on you, and give them this week what they truly need: time, attention, a meal, a word of encouragement.
2027-04-28.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Chief Shepherd of the flock, you are the same yesterday and today and forever. We remember before you your servant Isaac Mar Yoohanon, who spoke your word to your people and served at your altar. Forgive him every human weakness, and bring him to the city that is to come, to rejoice in the light of your face. Give your Church faithful and wise shepherds, who feed your household at the proper time. Make each of us a faithful steward of what you have entrusted to us, ready to be found at work when you come. Let us offer you a continual sacrifice of praise and never neglect to do good and to share. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: We have an altar: in the Holy Qurbono the one sacrifice of Christ, who suffered outside the gate to sanctify us by his own blood, is made present, and the faithful servants of every age are fed with his Body and Blood.

2027-04-29.title: Thursday of the fourth week after Qyomtho · St Catherine of Siena
readings: May the God of peace sanctify you entirely; the one who calls you is faithful
The wise and foolish bridesmaids: “Look! Here is the bridegroom!”
2027-04-29.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam remembers St Catherine of Siena, virgin and Doctor of the Church.
2027-04-29.verse: The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do this.
theo: The Gospel today is a wedding story, and it suits the saint the Church remembers. In Jesus' time the bridegroom came at night to bring his bride home, and young women of the village waited with lamps to light the procession. “Ten bridesmaids took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.” The difference is small and decisive: “the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps.” The bridegroom is delayed; all of them sleep. “But at midnight there was a shout, ‘Look! Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’” The lamps of the foolish are going out, and oil cannot be borrowed at the last moment. While they go to buy it, “the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went with him into the wedding banquet; and the door was shut.” Jesus ends: “Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.” St Augustine asked what the oil is, and answered that it is charity, the love that is not seen from outside but keeps the lamp burning; no one can lend another his love at the door (Sermon 93, in substance). St Ephrem and the Syriac Fathers loved to call Christ the Bridegroom and the Church his bride; in this Qyomtho season we know him as the risen Bridegroom, and he will come again. Is there oil in our lamps?

St Paul's blessing for the Thessalonians reads like a prayer for wise bridesmaids: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be kept sound and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Holiness is not only for the soul; the whole person, spirit, soul and body, is to be made ready for the Lord. That is why the Church cares for the body as well as the soul: in fasting and feasting, in chastity, in caring for the sick. Then comes the sentence that removes our fear: “The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do this.” We do not fill our lamps by our own strength. God who calls is faithful; he keeps pouring the oil of his grace through prayer and the sacraments, if we keep coming back for it. And Paul adds two very human requests: “Beloved, pray for us. Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss.” Holiness is never private. It grows in a community that prays for one another and shares the peace, as we do at the Qurbono when the kiss of peace passes from the altar through the whole church.

St Catherine of Siena was such a wise virgin. Born in 1347, one of the youngest of some twenty-five children of a dyer's family, she gave her life to Christ while still a girl and later joined the Dominican lay sisters of her city, the Mantellate. She nursed the sick in times of plague, visited prisoners, and gathered around her a circle of disciples. Though she had little schooling, she dictated a great book of spiritual teaching, the Dialogue, and some three hundred and eighty of her letters survive. With bold love she wrote to princes and to the Pope himself, and in 1376 she travelled to Avignon to beg Pope Gregory XI to return to Rome; he did so the next year. She died in Rome on 29 April 1380, at the age of thirty-three. Pope Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1970. Her lamp was full because she spent long hours with the Bridegroom in prayer; from that prayer came her fire for the Church. In one of her letters she wrote that if we are what we ought to be, we will set all Italy on fire (in substance). Ask her today for that fire, and for love of the Church and the Pope. Spend some time in prayer before the Most Holy Qurbono if you can: that is where the oil is given.
outline: Opening
Ask: if the Lord came tonight, would my lamp be burning?
Point 1 · Oil in the lamps
The wise and foolish bridesmaids; the oil that cannot be borrowed.
Point 2 · Sanctified entirely
Spirit, soul and body made ready; the faithful God who will do it.
Point 3 · St Catherine, a burning lamp
Prayer that became fire for the Church.
Take-home line
“The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do this.”
live: Fill your lamp (Matthew 25:4)
Spend fifteen minutes today in quiet prayer, before the Blessed Sacrament if you can, or at home before an icon.
Pray for us (1 Thessalonians 5:25)
Ask someone to pray for you this week, and pray daily for the Pope and our bishops, as St Catherine did.
2027-04-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen Bridegroom of the Church, you will come at an hour we do not know. Keep our lamps burning with the oil of your love, so that when the cry goes up at midnight we may go out to meet you and enter the wedding banquet with joy. God of peace, sanctify us entirely, spirit, soul and body, for you who call us are faithful. By the prayers of St Catherine of Siena, who spent herself in prayer and in love for your Church, kindle in us her fire, and bless our Holy Father the Pope and all the shepherds of your flock. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: The Bridegroom has already come to meet us: in the Holy Qurbono the risen Christ gives himself to his bride the Church, and fills our lamps with the oil of his love.

2027-04-30.title: Mar Yaqob Shleeha, son of Zebedee · St James the Apostle · Friday of the fourth week after Qyomtho
readings: Bear one another's burdens; let us not grow weary in doing what is right
“Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?”; the Son of Man came to serve
2027-04-30.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection), the week after the Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the feast of Mar Yaqob Shleeha, St James the Apostle, son of Zebedee and brother of St John.
2027-04-30.verse: For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.
theo: Today our Church keeps the feast of Mar Yaqob Shleeha, St James the son of Zebedee, the brother of St John. (He is not to be confused with the other apostle James, the son of Alphaeus.) The Byzantine Churches also honour him on this day; in the Latin Church his feast falls in July. James was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee who left his boat, his nets and his father to follow Jesus. With Peter and John he formed the inner circle of the Twelve: he saw the daughter of Jairus raised, he saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain, and he was taken close to him in the agony of Gethsemane. Jesus gave the two brothers a nickname, “Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder,” perhaps for their fiery temper. And he was the first of the apostles to die for Christ: the Acts of the Apostles records, in a single line, that King Herod “had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.” Our Church calls him Shleeha, the Syriac word for apostle, one who is sent.

The Gospel shows James before he understood. He and John come to Jesus with a bold request: “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you... Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” They are thinking of thrones. Jesus answers gently: “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?” They say at once, “We are able.” And Jesus says, “The cup that I drink you will drink.” St John Chrysostom notes that the Lord did not scold them, but led them gently from the thought of honour to the thought of the cup, from the throne to the share in his sufferings (Homilies on Matthew 65, in substance). The other ten are angry, and Jesus gathers them all: among the nations, rulers “lord it over them,” “But it is not so among you; but whoever wishes to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you must be slave of all. For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.” James learned the lesson. A little more than ten years after the Resurrection he drank the cup. Clement of Alexandria, as Eusebius records, tells that the man who brought James to trial was so moved by his witness that he confessed himself a Christian; as they were led out together, he asked James to forgive him, and James said, “Peace be with you,” and kissed him; and both were beheaded (Church History II.9, in substance).

St Paul's words to the Galatians show what the cup and the service look like in an ordinary parish. “My friends, if anyone is detected in a transgression, you who have received the Spirit should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” Not gossip, not public shaming, but gentle restoring, as James restored his accuser with a kiss. “Bear one another's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.” Each of us “must carry their own loads,” and yet we help carry each other's. And Paul adds the farmer's law: “you reap whatever you sow... So let us not grow weary in doing what is right, for we will reap at harvest time, if we do not give up.” In Kerala many parishes and families bear the name of St James, and many pilgrims know the long road to his shrine at Compostela in Spain, where by an old tradition his relics are venerated. The road that matters most, though, is the one from the throne we would like to the cup we are given. Today, serve someone who cannot repay you; gently restore someone who has fallen; and carry one burden that is not your own. That is to drink the Lord's cup and to share his glory.
conn: The cup and the sword.
Mark 10:39 and Acts 12:2: Jesus foretold that James would drink his cup; James was the first of the Twelve to die for him.
The servant who gives his life.
Mark 10:45 echoes the Servant of Isaiah 53, who bears the iniquities of many; the apostles share in his service.
Restoring with gentleness.
Galatians 6:1 and the account of James forgiving his accuser with the words “Peace be with you.”
fathers: St John Chrysostom

The Lord did not rebuke the sons of Zebedee harshly, but led them from the desire of honours to the cup, that is, to fellowship in his sufferings, and so prepared them for true glory (Homilies on Matthew 65, in substance).
Clement of Alexandria (in Eusebius)

The man who had brought James to trial, moved by his witness, confessed himself a Christian; on the way to death he asked for forgiveness, and James said, Peace be with you, and kissed him; and both were beheaded together (Eusebius, Church History II.9, in substance).
magis: Catechism 622
The redemption won by Christ consists in this: he came “to give his life as a ransom for many,” loving his own to the end so that they might be ransomed from sin.
Catechism 786
Christ exercised his kingship by drawing all to himself through his death and Resurrection; for the Christian, to reign is to serve him, especially in the poor and the suffering.
Catechism 2473
Martyrdom is the supreme witness to the truth of the faith: the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose.
outline: Opening
Ask: if Jesus asked me today, what do you want me to do for you, what would I say?
Point 1 · Grant us to sit at your right and your left
The thrones James wanted and the cup he was given.
Point 2 · The Son of Man came to serve
Greatness in the kingdom is service; the ransom for many.
Point 3 · Bear one another's burdens
Gentle restoring, shared loads, and not growing weary.
Take-home line
“The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.”
live: Serve someone who cannot repay you (Mark 10:43–45)
Today do one hidden act of service for someone who cannot return it.
Carry another's burden (Galatians 6:2)
This week, take on one burden of a family member, neighbour or colleague without being asked.
2027-04-30.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you came not to be served but to serve and to give your life as a ransom for many. You called Mar Yaqob from his boat and nets, bore with his ambition, and taught him to drink your cup; he became the first of your apostles to give his life for you. By his prayers deliver us from the desire to sit in the first places, and make us servants of one another. Teach us to restore those who fall with gentleness, to bear one another's burdens, and never to grow weary in doing good. Bring us at last to share your glory. You live and reign for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Lord gives us the cup he drank: the Blood of the new covenant poured out for many. In the Holy Qurbono we share in the Servant's sacrifice and receive strength to serve.

quick: The risen Lord gives peace, mission, the Spirit and forgiveness.
Thomas' doubt becomes the great confession: “My Lord and my God!”
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe: that is us.
2027-04-04.action: Say “My Lord and my God” at the elevation in every Qurbono.
2027-04-04.question: Where are the locked doors in my life that Jesus wants to enter?
2027-04-04.special: New Sunday: the appearance of the risen Lord to the apostles and to Thomas.
illus: An illustration
Pilgrims at the shrine of St Thomas in Mylapore kneel and whisper “My Lord and my God.” A faith that crossed seas from a doubting apostle's touch has lasted nearly two thousand years in our land.

family.explain: Thomas did not believe Jesus had risen until he saw him. When Jesus showed him his hands and side, Thomas said: “My Lord and my God!” Thomas later came to India to tell people about Jesus.
family.intention: We thank God for St Thomas who brought the faith to India.
family.ask: Ask: “Why do we call ourselves St Thomas Christians?”

catechism: The apostles meet the risen Lord.
kidsaint: He wanted to see before believing, but when he met the risen Jesus he said: “My Lord and my God!” Tradition says he brought the Gospel to India. Lesson: bring your questions to Jesus; he helps you believe.
term: The Sunday after Qyomtho, also called Thomas Sunday, when the Church reads the appearances of the risen Lord to the apostles and to Thomas (John 20:19–29).
termMore: The ancient Christians of Kerala trace their faith to the preaching of St Thomas. The Syro-Malankara and Syro-Malabar Churches both belong to this heritage.

quick: The risen Lord meets us in our empty nights.
“Come and have breakfast”: he feeds us at his table.
“Do you love me?”: love restores us after failure.
2027-04-11.action: Each night this week, tell Jesus: “Lord, you know that I love you.”
2027-04-11.question: Have I let a failure stop me from following Jesus?
illus: An illustration

Fishermen on Kerala's coast know nights when the boats come back empty. Then a call comes: “Fish to the north!” and the nets come back full. The disciples knew that morning; the risen Lord still turns our empty nights into full nets.

family.explain: The disciples caught nothing all night. Jesus told them where to throw the net, and it became full of fish! Then Jesus made them breakfast on the beach.
family.intention: We pray for fishermen and for all who work hard and feel they have failed.
family.ask: Ask: “When have we felt that we failed, and how did God help us?”

kidsaint: He denied Jesus three times, but Jesus forgave him and asked three times: “Do you love me?” Peter became the leader of the Church. Lesson: when you fail, come back to Jesus and say “I love you.”
term: The fifty days from Easter to Pentecost, kept as one great feast of the Resurrection. Its Sundays read the appearances of the risen Lord.
termMore: Many of the apostles were fishermen. After the Resurrection Jesus meets them at their work and makes them “fishers of people” for good.

quick: Jesus walks with us even when we do not recognise him.
Our hearts burn in the Word; our eyes open in the breaking of the bread.
Meeting the risen Lord, we cannot keep silent.
2027-04-18.action: Read the Sunday Gospel every day this week.
2027-04-18.question: On which road of disappointment do I need to recognise Jesus walking beside me?
2027-04-18.special: Third Sunday after Qyomtho: the disciples of Emmaus.
illus: An illustration

A Kerala nurse working abroad felt lost and stopped going to church. One evening a stranger from her parish town invited her to an Indian Qurbono nearby. When the priest broke the bread, she wept: “I felt I was home.” Emmaus happens still.

family.explain: Two sad friends walked with a stranger who explained the Bible to them. When he broke bread at supper, they saw it was Jesus! They ran back to tell everyone.
family.intention: We pray for people who feel sad or lost, that they may meet Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “Where did we feel Jesus close to us this week?”

catechism: Scripture in the life of the Church.
kidsaint: He wrote the shortest Gospel, full of action, so that people everywhere could know Jesus. His Gospel tells how the risen Jesus appeared to two disciples on the road. Lesson: read a little of the Gospel every day.
term: A village about eleven kilometres from Jerusalem, where two disciples recognised the risen Lord in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:13–35). The story is a picture of every Holy Qurbono.
termMore: The Fathers spoke of two tables in the liturgy: the table of the Word and the table of the Body of Christ. Both nourish us.
